=== Maintenance ===
Nearly every modern air conditioning system, even small window package units, is equipped with an internal air filter or electrostatic precipitator. The filters may range from a lightweight gauze-like material to a heavier-duty pleated mat composed of borosilicate glass fibers. Filters are typically replaced or washed as conditions warrant. For example, a building in a dusty environment or a home with furry pets will need to have the filters changed more often than interior spaces without these dirt loads. Failure to replace these filters as needed can contribute to a lower heat exchange rate, resulting in wasted energy, shortened equipment life, and higher energy bills. Low airflow can result in iced-over evaporator coils, which can completely stop airflow. Additionally, very dirty or plugged filters can cause overheating during a heating cycle, which can result in damage to the system or even fire.

Because an air conditioner moves heat between the indoor coil and the outdoor coil, both must be kept clean. This means that, in addition to replacing the air filter at the evaporator coil, it is also necessary to regularly clean the condenser coil. Failure to keep the condenser clean will eventually result in harm to the compressor because the condenser coil is responsible for discharging both the indoor heat (as picked up by the evaporator) and the heat generated by the electric motor driving the compressor.<ref>{{cite web |title=Maintaining Your Air Conditioner |url=https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/maintaining-your-air-conditioner |publisher=U.S. Department of Energy |access-date=16 October 2025}}</ref>

==Energy efficiency==
HVAC systems play a key role in improving the energy efficiency of buildings, as the building sector accounts for one of the highest shares of global energy consumption.<ref>Chenari, B., Dias Carrilho, J. and Gameiro da Silva, M., 2016. Towards sustainable, energy-efficient and healthy ventilation strategies in buildings: A review. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 59, pp.1426-1447.</ref> Since the 1980s, HVAC equipment manufacturers have focused on improving system efficiency. Initially, these efforts were driven by rising energy costs, but in recent years, environmental sustainability and stricter efficiency regulations have become the primary motivators. Additionally, improving HVAC system efficiency can enhance indoor air quality, which may lead to better occupant health, comfort, and productivity.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sustainable Facilities Tool: HVAC System Overview|url=https://sftool.gov/explore/green-building/section/9/hvac/system-overview|website=sftool.gov|access-date=2 July 2014}}</ref> In the US, the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|EPA]] has imposed tighter restrictions over the years. There are several methods for making HVAC systems more efficient.

===Heating energy===
In the past, water heating was more efficient for heating buildings and was the standard in the United States. Today, [[forced air]] systems can double for air conditioning and are more popular.

Energy efficiency can be improved in central heating systems by using zoned heating. This allows a more granular application of heat, similar to non-central heating systems. Zones are controlled by multiple thermostats. In water heating systems the thermostats control [[zone valve]]s, and in forced air systems they control [[zone damper]]s inside the vents which selectively block the flow of air. 

[[Forecasting (heating)|Forecasting]] is another method of controlling building heating by calculating the demand for heating energy that should be supplied to the building in each time unit.

===Ground source heat pump===
{{Main|Geothermal heat pump}}
Ground source, or geothermal, heat pumps are similar to ordinary heat pumps, but instead of transferring heat to or from outside air, they rely on the stable, even temperature of the earth to provide heating and air conditioning. Many regions experience seasonal temperature extremes, which would require large-capacity heating and cooling equipment to heat or cool buildings. For example, a conventional heat pump system used to heat a building in Montana's {{convert|-70|°F|°C|lk=off|order=flip}} low temperature or cool a building in the highest temperature ever recorded in the US—{{convert|134|°F|°C|order=flip}} in [[Death Valley]], California, in 1913 would require a large amount of energy due to the extreme difference between inside and outside air temperatures. A metre below the earth's surface, however, the ground remains at a relatively constant temperature. Utilizing this large source of relatively moderate temperature earth, a heating or cooling system's capacity can often be significantly reduced. Although ground temperatures vary according to latitude, at {{convert|6|ft|m|order=flip}} underground, temperatures generally only range from {{convert|45|to|75|°F|°C|order=flip}}.

===Solar air conditioning===
{{Main|Solar air conditioning}}
Photovoltaic solar panels can potentially decrease the operating cost of air conditioning. Traditional air conditioners run using alternating current, and hence, any direct-current solar power needs to be inverted to be compatible with these units. New variable-speed DC-motor units allow solar power to more easily run them since this conversion is unnecessary, and since the motors are tolerant of voltage fluctuations associated with variance in supplied solar power (e.g., due to cloud cover).

===Ventilation energy recovery===
[[Energy recovery]] systems sometimes utilize [[heat recovery ventilation]] or [[energy recovery ventilation]] systems that employ [[heat exchanger]]s or [[thermal wheel|enthalpy wheels]] to recover [[sensible heat|sensible]] or [[latent heat]] from exhausted air. This is done by transfer of energy from the stale air inside the home to the incoming fresh air from outside.

===Air conditioning energy===
The performance of vapor compression refrigeration cycles is limited by [[Second law of thermodynamics|thermodynamics]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nuclear-power.net/nuclear-engineering/thermodynamics/thermodynamic-cycles/heating-and-air-conditioning/#Vapor-compression_Cycle_8211_Vapor-compression_Refrigeration|title=Heating and Air Conditioning|website=www.nuclear-power.net|language=en-US|access-date=2018-02-10}}</ref> These air conditioning and heat pump devices ''move'' heat rather than convert it from one form to another, so ''[[Thermal efficiency|thermal efficiencies]]'' do not appropriately describe the performance of these devices. The [[Coefficient of performance]] (COP) measures performance, but this dimensionless measure has not been adopted. Instead, the Energy Efficiency Ratio (''EER'') has traditionally been used to characterize the performance of many HVAC systems. EER is the Energy Efficiency Ratio based on a {{convert|35|C|F}} outdoor temperature. To more accurately describe the performance of air conditioning equipment over a typical cooling season a modified version of the EER, the Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio (''SEER''), or in Europe the [[ESEER]], is used. SEER ratings are based on seasonal temperature averages instead of a constant {{convert|35|°C}} outdoor temperature. The current industry minimum SEER rating is 14 SEER.{{citation needed|date=December 2019}} Engineers have pointed out some areas where efficiency of the existing hardware could be improved. For example, the fan blades used to move the air are usually stamped from sheet metal, an economical method of manufacture, but as a result they are not aerodynamically efficient. A well-designed blade could reduce the electrical power required to move the air by a third.<ref>[https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2010/07/15/keeping-cool-and-green Keeping cool and green], ''[[The Economist]]'' 17 July 2010, p. 83</ref>

=== Demand-controlled kitchen ventilation ===
{{main|Demand controlled ventilation}}
Demand-controlled kitchen ventilation (DCKV) is a building controls approach to controlling the volume of kitchen exhaust and supply air in response to the actual cooking loads in a commercial kitchen. Traditional commercial kitchen ventilation systems operate at 100% fan speed independent of the volume of cooking activity and DCKV technology changes that to provide significant fan energy and conditioned air savings. By deploying smart sensing technology, both the exhaust and supply fans can be controlled to capitalize on the [[affinity laws]] for motor energy savings, reduce makeup air heating and cooling energy, increasing safety, and reducing ambient kitchen noise levels.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/dckv_technology_profile.pdf|title=Technology Profile: Demand Control Kitchen Ventilation (DCKV)|access-date=2018-12-04}}</ref>

==Air filtration and cleaning==
{{Main|Air filter}}
[[File:Air handling unit.JPG|thumb|[[Air handling unit]], used for heating, cooling, and filtering the air]]
Air cleaning and filtration removes particles, contaminants, vapors and gases from the air. The filtered and cleaned air then is used in heating, ventilation, and air conditioning.

Clean air delivery rate (CADR) is the amount of clean air an air cleaner provides to a room or space. When determining CADR, the amount of airflow in a space is taken into account. For example, an air cleaner with a flow rate of {{convert|30|m3|ft3|sigfig=1}} per minute and an efficiency of 50% has a CADR of {{convert|15|m3|ft3|sigfig=1}} per minute. Filtration performance determines the fraction of airborne particles, including allergens, bacteria, and fine particulate matter, removed from recirculated air. This depends on the size of the particle or fiber, the filter packing density and depth, and the airflow rate.<ref name="Howard 2003 1–63">{{citation |last=Howard |first=J |title=Guidance for Filtration and Air-Cleaning Systems to Protect Building Environments from Airborne Chemical, Biological, or Radiological Attacks |publisher=[[National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health]] |year=2003 |id=2003-136 |url=https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/docs/2003-136/|doi=10.26616/NIOSHPUB2003136 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Industry and standards ==
The HVAC industry includes equipment manufacturing, system design, installation, operation, maintenance, sales, education, and research. The HVAC industry was historically regulated by the manufacturers of HVAC equipment, but regulating and standards organizations such as HARDI (Heating, Air-conditioning and Refrigeration Distributors International), [[ASHRAE]], [[SMACNA]], ACCA (Air Conditioning Contractors of America), [[Uniform Mechanical Code]], [[International Building Code|International Mechanical Code]], and [[Air Movement and Control Association|AMCA]] have been established to support the industry. [[United Laboratories|UL]] is an omnibus agency and is not specific to the HVAC industry.

=== International ===
ISO 16813:2006 is one of the [[International Organization for Standardization|ISO]] building environment standards.<ref>{{cite web|last=ISO|title=Building environment standards|url=http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_tc_browse.htm?commid=54740|publisher=www.iso.org|access-date=2011-05-14}}</ref> It establishes the general principles of building environment design. It takes into account the need to provide a healthy indoor environment for the occupants as well as the need to protect the environment for future generations and promote collaboration among the various parties involved in building environmental design for sustainability. ISO16813 is applicable to new construction and the retrofit of existing buildings.<ref name=iso16813>{{cite web | author=ISO | title=Building environment design—Indoor environment—General principles | url=http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=41300 | access-date=14 May 2011}}</ref>

The building environmental design standard aims to:<ref name=iso16813 />
* provide the constraints concerning sustainability issues from the initial stage of the design process, with building and plant life cycle to be considered together with owning and operating costs from the beginning of the design process;
* assess the proposed design with rational criteria for indoor air quality, thermal comfort, acoustical comfort, visual comfort, energy efficiency, and HVAC system controls at every stage of the design process;
* iterate decisions and evaluations of the design throughout the design process.

==== Societies ====
{{See Also|American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers}}
{{See Also|Air Conditioning, Heating and Refrigeration Institute}}

Many HVAC engineers are members of the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating, and Air-Conditioning Engineers ([[ASHRAE]]). ASHRAE publishes recognized standards for HVAC design, which are updated every four years.<ref>{{Cite web|title=ASHRAE Handbook Online|url=https://www.ashrae.org/technical-resources/ashrae-handbook/ashrae-handbook-online|access-date=2020-06-17|website=www.ashrae.org}}</ref> Another popular society is [[AHRI]], which provides regular information on new refrigeration technology, and publishes relevant [[AHRI Standard 700|standards]] and codes.

==== Codes ====
American design standards are legislated in the [[Uniform Mechanical Code]] or International Mechanical Code. In certain states, counties, or cities, either of these codes may be adopted and amended via various legislative processes. These codes are updated and published by the International Association of Plumbing and Mechanical Officials ([[IAPMO]]) or the International Code Council ([[International Code Council|ICC]]) respectively, on a 3-year code development cycle. Typically, local building permit departments are charged with enforcement of these standards on private and certain public properties.

==== Technicians ====

An '''HVAC technician''' is a [[tradesman]] who specializes in heating, ventilation, air conditioning, and refrigeration. HVAC technicians in the US can receive training through formal training institutions, where most earn [[associate degree]]s. Training for HVAC technicians includes classroom lectures and hands-on tasks, and can be followed by an apprenticeship wherein the recent graduate works alongside a professional HVAC technician for a temporary period.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Heating, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration Mechanics and Installers : Occupational Outlook Handbook: : U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics |url=https://www.bls.gov/ooh/installation-maintenance-and-repair/heating-air-conditioning-and-refrigeration-mechanics-and-installers.htm#tab-4 |access-date=2023-06-22 |website=www.bls.gov |language=en-us}}</ref> HVAC techs who have been trained can also be certified in areas such as air conditioning, heat pumps, gas heating, and commercial refrigeration.

=== United Kingdom ===
The [[Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers]] is a body that covers the essential [[Service (systems architecture)]] that allow buildings to operate. It includes the electrotechnical, [[heating]], [[ventilating]], air conditioning, refrigeration and [[plumbing]] industries. To train as a [[Building services engineering|building services engineer]], the typical [[Academy|academic]] entry requirements include qualifications in mathematics and science, such as GCSEs (A-C) in England or Standard Grades (1-3) in Scotland. Employers will often want a [[academic degree|degree]] in a branch of [[engineering]], such as building environment engineering, electrical engineering or mechanical engineering. To become a full member of CIBSE, and so also to be registered by the [[Engineering Council UK]] as a chartered engineer, engineers must also attain an Honours Degree and a master's degree in a relevant engineering subject.{{citation needed|date=December 2019}} CIBSE publishes several guides to HVAC design relevant to the UK market, and also the Republic of Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and Hong Kong. These guides include various recommended design criteria and standards, some of which are cited within the UK building regulations, and therefore form a legislative requirement for major building services works. The main guides are:

* Guide A: Environmental Design
* Guide B: Heating, Ventilating, Air Conditioning and Refrigeration
* Guide C: Reference Data
* Guide D: Transportation systems in Buildings
* Guide E: Fire Safety Engineering
* Guide F: Energy Efficiency in Buildings
* Guide G: Public Health Engineering
* Guide H: Building Control Systems
* Guide J: Weather, Solar and Illuminance Data
* Guide K: Electricity in Buildings
* Guide L: Sustainability
* Guide M: Maintenance Engineering and Management

Within the [[construction]] sector, it is the job of the building services engineer to [[design]] and oversee the installation and maintenance of the essential services such as gas, [[electricity]], water, heating and [[lighting]]. Building Services is part of a sector that has over 51,000 businesses and represents 2–3% of the [[GDP]].

=== Australia ===
The Air Conditioning and Mechanical Contractors Association of Australia (AMCA), Australian Institute of Refrigeration, Air Conditioning and Heating (AIRAH), Australian Refrigeration Mechanical Association and CIBSE are responsible.

=== Asia ===
Asian architectural temperature-control have different priorities than European methods. For example, Asian heating traditionally focuses on maintaining [[Underfloor heating#History|temperatures of objects such as the floor]] or furnishings such as [[Kotatsu]] tables and directly warming people, as opposed to the Western focus, in modern periods, on designing air systems.

==== Philippines ====
The Philippine Society of Ventilating, Air Conditioning and Refrigerating Engineers (PSVARE) along with Philippine Society of Mechanical Engineers (PSME) govern on the codes and standards for HVAC / MVAC (MVAC means "mechanical ventilation and air conditioning") in the Philippines.

====India====
The Indian Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air Conditioning Engineers (ISHRAE) was established to promote the HVAC industry in India. ISHRAE is an associate of ASHRAE. ISHRAE was founded at [[New Delhi]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ishrae.in/Home/about_ishrae |title=About ISHRAE |publisher=ISHRAE |access-date=2021-10-11}}</ref> in 1981 and a chapter was started in Bangalore in 1989. Between 1989 & 1993, ISHRAE chapters were formed in all major cities in India.{{citation needed|date=November 2019}}

'''The Home Depot, Inc.''' is an American [[multinational corporation|multinational]] [[home improvement]] retail corporation which sells [[tool]]s, [[construction]] products, building materials, appliances, and services including fuel and transportation rentals. Home Depot is the largest home improvement specialty retailer in the United States.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Ausick|first1=Paul|title=Why Home Depot Dominates the Home Improvement Market|url=http://247wallst.com/retail/2017/03/09/why-home-depot-dominates-the-home-improvement-market/|work=24/7 Wall St|access-date=July 19, 2019|date=March 9, 2017}}</ref> In fiscal 2024, the company reported $159.5 billion in revenue and approximately 470,100 associates.<ref>{{cite web |title=2024 Annual Report |url=https://ir.homedepot.com/~/media/Files/H/HomeDepot-IR/2025/HD_2024_AR_IRsite_v2.pdf |publisher=The Home Depot, Inc. |access-date=March 13, 2026}}</ref> The company is headquartered in [[Cobb County, Georgia]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.wsbtv.com/news/local/cobb-county/home-depot-seeks-tax-break-140m-expansion-project-cobb-county/HKYZL2DYZ5E5VIFT7IVT6VCVBY/|title=Home Depot seeks tax break on $140M expansion project in Cobb County|publisher=[[WSB-TV]]|date=2025-09-17|access-date=2025-12-14|quote=Cobb County-based Home Depot[...]}}</ref> with an [[Atlanta]] mailing address.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ir.homedepot.com/investor-resources/contact-investor-relations|title=Contact Investor Relations|publisher=The Home Depot|access-date=2025-12-14|quote=2455 Paces Ferry Road Atlanta, GA 30339}} - The address is under the tab "I would like to submit a question or comment to the investor relations department."</ref>

Home Depot operates many [[big-box store|big-box format stores]] across the United States (including the [[District of Columbia]], [[Guam]], [[Puerto Rico]] and the [[United States Virgin Islands|U.S. Virgin Islands]]); all 10 provinces of Canada; and all 31 Mexican states and [[Mexico City]]. Interline Brands ([[The Home Depot Pro]]), a maintenance, repair, and operations company is also owned by The Home Depot, with 70 distribution centers across the United States. It is the seventh [[List of largest United States–based employers globally|largest United States–based employer globally]].

==History==
===1978–1999===
The Home Depot was co-founded by [[Bernard Marcus]], [[Arthur Blank]], [[Ron Brill]], [[Pat Farrah]], and [[Ken Langone]] in 1978.<ref name="Corporate history">{{cite web|url=http://corporate.homedepot.com/wps/portal/!ut/p/c1/04_SB8K8xLLM9MSSzPy8xBz9CP0os3gDdwNHH0sfE3M3AzMPJ8MAV0sDKADKR2LKmxrD5fHr9vPIz03VL8iNKAcAodaFaQ!!/dl2/d1/L2dJQSEvUUt3QS9ZQnB3LzZfMEcwQUw5TDQ3RjA2SEIxUEY5MDAwMDAwMDA!/|publisher=Home Depot Corporate website: Our History|title=Home Depot Corporate website: Our History|access-date=June 11, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090626125227/http://corporate.homedepot.com/wps/portal/!ut/p/c1/04_SB8K8xLLM9MSSzPy8xBz9CP0os3gDdwNHH0sfE3M3AzMPJ8MAV0sDKADKR2LKmxrD5fHr9vPIz03VL8iNKAcAodaFaQ!!/dl2/d1/L2dJQSEvUUt3QS9ZQnB3LzZfMEcwQUw5TDQ3RjA2SEIxUEY5MDAwMDAwMDA!/|archive-date=June 26, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Profile: Ken Langone |url=https://www.forbes.com/profile/ken-langone/?sh=2fd5fc9385c1 |work=[[Forbes]]|access-date=29 June 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=KEN LANGONE: THE GENEROSITY OF TIME |url=https://corporate.homedepot.com/newsroom/ken-langone-generosity-time |website=Home Depot Corporate |access-date=26 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=1994-12-28 |title=Home Depot to Open in S.L. |url=https://www.deseret.com/1994/12/28/19150254/home-depot-to-open-in-s-l/ |access-date=2025-06-23 |website=Deseret News |language=en}}</ref> The Home Depot's proposition was to build home-improvement [[Big-box store|superstore]]s, larger than any of its competitors' facilities.  Investment banker Ken Langone helped Marcus and Blank to secure the necessary [[Financial capital|capital]].
[[File:Home-Depot-at-Atlanta-Store-Support-Center.jpg|thumb|The Home Depot [[Atlanta]] Store Support Center, 2018.]]
On June 22, 1979, the first two stores, built in spaces leased from [[J. C. Penney]] that were originally [[The Treasury (retailer)|Treasure Island]] "[[hypermarket]]" ([[discount department store|discount department]] and [[grocery store|grocery]]) stores, opened in [[metro Atlanta]] (in [[Doraville]] and on [[Memorial Drive (Atlanta)|Memorial Drive]] in [[Decatur, Georgia|Decatur]], both near [[I-285 (GA)|I-285]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ext.homedepot.com/community/blog/on-the-anniversary-of-the-first-stores-remembering-the-home-depots-roots/|title=Home Depot History|publisher=ext.homedepot.com|access-date=September 3, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140904180937/http://ext.homedepot.com/community/blog/on-the-anniversary-of-the-first-stores-remembering-the-home-depots-roots/|archive-date=September 4, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://corporate.homedepot.com/sites/default/themes/thd/images/timeline/History-Of-The-Home-Depot.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161019124234/https://corporate.homedepot.com/sites/default/themes/thd/images/timeline/History-Of-The-Home-Depot.pdf |title=History of The Home Depot |archive-date=October 19, 2016 |publisher=The Home Depot |access-date=August 20, 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/home-depot-first-stores-photos-2019-4#as-a-result-of-the-deal-with-jcpenney-home-depot-launched-two-initial-stores-7|title = Here's what Home Depot looked like when it first opened in 1979| website=[[Business Insider]] }}</ref> On September 22, 1981, The Home Depot went public on the [[NASDAQ]], raising $4.093 million. The Home Depot joined the [[New York Stock Exchange]] on April 19, 1984.<ref>{{cite web|title=Investor FAQ|url=http://ir.homedepot.com/phoenix.zhtml?c=63646&p=irol-faq|website=The Home Depot, Inc.|access-date=April 11, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160123220127/http://ir.homedepot.com/phoenix.zhtml?c=63646&p=irol-faq|archive-date=January 23, 2016}}</ref>

The Home Depot began to branch out of Georgia to Florida in 1981 with stores opening in [[Hollywood, Florida|Hollywood]] and [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida|Fort Lauderdale]]. By 1984, The Home Depot was operating 19 stores with sales of over $256 million. To enter the [[Dallas]] market The Home Depot acquired Bowater Home Center from Bowater Inc. on October 31, 1984, for $40 million.<ref>{{cite news|title=Home Depot|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/10/31/business/home-depot.html|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=October 31, 1984}}</ref> The increased expansion of The Home Depot in the mid-1980s created financial difficulties with earnings falling by 42% and debt rising to $200 million. The financial difficulties of The Home Depot also caused the stock price to fall. Only 10 stores were opened in 1986, with a stock offering of 2.99 million shares at $17 per share. This helped the company restructure its debts.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Home Depot, Inc. – Company Profile |url=http://www.referenceforbusiness.com/history2/23/The-Home-Depot-Inc.html|access-date=April 21, 2017}}</ref>

[[File:A Home Depot store in Blairsville, Ga.jpg|thumb|A Home Depot store in [[Blairsville, Georgia]]]]

In 1989, The Home Depot became the largest home improvement store in the United States, surpassing [[Lowe's]]. In the 1990s, The Home Depot searched for ways to redefine its marketplace. The EXPO Design Center subsidiary was launched in 1991 to provide high-end products and design services. A 480-page book, ''Home Improvement 1-2-3'', was published in 1995.

The Canadian hardware chain [[Aikenhead's Hardware]] was acquired by The Home Depot in 1994 for $150 million with a 75% share. All of the Aikenhead's Hardware stores were later converted to The Home Depot stores.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Strom|first1=Stephanie|title=COMPANY NEWS; Home Depot Buys Chain In Canada|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/02/09/business/company-news-home-depot-buys-chain-in-canada.html|access-date=April 21, 2017|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=February 9, 1994}}</ref> By 1995, sales reached $10 billion while operating 350 stores. Former [[General Electric]] executive [[Robert Nardelli]] became CEO and president of The Home Depot in 2000.<ref>{{cite news|title=Home Depot Names GE's Nardelli As New CEO in a Surprise Move|newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|date=December 6, 2000|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB976051062408860254|access-date=April 22, 2017}}</ref>

===2000–2007===
[[San Diego]] maintenance and repair supplies company Maintenance Warehouse was purchased by The Home Depot in 1997 for $245 million.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/01/28/business/home-depot-to-pay-245.4-million-for-direct-marketer.html|title=Home Depot to Pay $245.4 Million for Direct Marketer|date=January 28, 1997|work=[[The New York Times]]|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Maintenance Warehouse was a leading direct-mail marketer of maintenance, repair and operations supplies that could reach customers out of reach by The Home Depot.<ref>{{cite news|title=Home Depot Plans To Buy Maintenance Warehouse|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/01/17/business/home-depot-plans-to-buy-maintenance-warehouse.html|access-date=April 22, 2017|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=January 17, 1997}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.pmmag.com/articles/84784-home-depot-tightens-focus-on-commercial-customers|title=Home Depot Tightens Focus on Commercial Customers|work=Plumbing & Mechanical|access-date=April 22, 2017|year=1997}}</ref> Atlanta-based company Apex Supply was acquired by The Home Depot in 1999. Apex Supply is a wholesale distributor of plumbing, HVAC, industrial pipe and fittings.<ref>{{cite news|title=Home Depot to acquire Apex Supply Co.|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/atlanta/stories/1999/12/13/daily1.html|access-date=April 22, 2017|newspaper=Atlanta Business Chronicle|date=December 13, 1999}}</ref> Apex Supply and Maintenance Warehouse stores were rebranded in 2004 as "The Home Depot Supply".<ref>{{cite news|title=New Name For Apex Supply Co. And Maintenance Warehouse|url=https://www.supplyht.com/articles/87567-new-name-for-apex-supply-co-and-maintenance-warehouse|access-date=April 22, 2017|publisher=Supply House Times|date=March 1, 2004}}</ref>

In 2004, Home Depot employees at a suburban Detroit store in [[Harper Woods, Michigan]], rejected a bid to be represented by a [[labor union]], voting 115 to 42 against joining the [[United Food and Commercial Workers]]. If the union had won, the Michigan store would have been the first Home Depot to have union representation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.floordaily.net/flooring-news/Home_Depot_Workers_Reject_Bid_to_Unionize.aspx|title=Home Depot Workers Reject Bid to Unionize|publisher=Floordaily.net|access-date=October 16, 2022}}</ref>

Your Other Warehouse, a large plumbing distributor with a focus on special order fulfillment, was acquired by The Home Depot in 2001. Your Other Warehouse also supplied two divisions of The Home Depot and the EXPO Design Centers.<ref>{{cite news|title=Home Depot to acquire Your "other" Warehouse|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/atlanta/stories/2001/10/01/daily21.html|access-date=April 22, 2017|newspaper=Atlanta Business Chronicle|date=October 3, 2001}}</ref> The "EXPO Design Center" division was reorganized in 2001 with three divisions based in the Northeast at [[South Plainfield, New Jersey]], the West at [[Orange, California]], and the Southeast at [[Atlanta, Georgia]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Home Depot To Redesign EXPO Division|url=https://vmsd.com/home-depot-to-redesign-expo-division/|access-date=April 22, 2017|publisher=[[VMSD]]|date=September 11, 2000}}</ref>

The Home Depot entered the [[Mexico|Mexican]] market in 2002 with the acquisition of the home improvement chain Del Norte. In addition, The Home Depot had begun construction of stores in [[Mexicali]] and [[Tijuana]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Home Depot acquires Del Norte|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/atlanta/stories/2002/03/18/daily24.html|access-date=April 22, 2017|newspaper=Atlanta Business Chronicle|date=March 21, 2002}}</ref> In the same year the [[Home Depot Landscape Supply]] was launched to integrate professional landscapers and upscale plants into a [[plant nursery]] retail chain. Home Depot Landscape Supply lasted only five years with only a few stores each in metro Atlanta and [[Dallas/Fort Worth]]. The Home Depot decided to close all Home Depot Landscape Supply stores in late 2007.<ref>{{cite news|title=Home Depot Closing Landscape Supply Stores|url=https://chainstoreage.com/real-estate/home-depot-closing-landscape-supply-stores|access-date=October 16, 2022|publisher=Chain Store Age}}</ref>

In September 2005, Home Depot Direct launched its online home-furnishings store, 10 Crescent Lane, shortly followed by the launch of "Paces Trading Company", its online lighting store. In mid-2006, the Home Depot acquired Home Decorators Collection, which was placed as an additional brand under its Home Depot Direct division.

In 2006, the Home Depot acquired [[Hughes Supply]], the largest home construction wholesaler in the United States for $3.2 billion.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Funk|first1=Dale|title=Home Depot to buy Hughes Supply for about $3.2 billion|url=https://www.ewweb.com/news/mergers-acquisitions/article/20920343/home-depot-to-buy-hughes-supply-for-about-32-billion|access-date=April 22, 2017|publisher=Electrical Wholesaling|date=January 1, 2006}}</ref> Hughes Supply was integrated into The Home Depot Supply to better serve business-to-business customers.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Home Depot Completes Acquisition of Hughes Supply|url=https://www.contractingbusiness.com/archive/article/20864018/the-home-depot-completes-acquisition-of-hughes-supply|access-date=April 22, 2017|publisher=Contracting Business|date=April 1, 2006}}</ref> The Home Depot Supply rebranded under the new name [[HD Supply]] in January 2007.<ref>{{cite news|title=Wholesale Division of Home Depot Branded Under Name of HD Supply|url=https://www.achrnews.com/articles/103642-wholesale-division-of-home-depot-branded-under-name-of-hd-supply|access-date=April 22, 2017|publisher=Achrnews|date=January 29, 2007}}</ref> Five months later, The Home Depot sold HD Supply to a consortium of three [[private equity]] firms, [[The Carlyle Group]], [[Bain Capital]] and [[Clayton, Dubilier and Rice]] (with each agreeing to buy a one-third stake in the division).<ref>{{cite web|last=Alden|first=William|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/dealbook.nytimes.com/2013/04/12/hd-supply-backed-by-carlyle-and-bain-files-for-i-p-o/|title=HD Supply, Backed by Carlyle and Bain, Files for I.P.O.|work=[[DealBook]]|date=April 12, 2013|access-date=October 16, 2022}}</ref>

===Since 2007===
[[File:Home Depot, center aisle, Natick MA.jpg|thumb|upright|Center aisle of a Home Depot store in 2014]]

On January 2, 2007, The Home Depot and [[Robert Nardelli]] mutually agreed on Nardelli's resignation as CEO after a six-year tenure. Nardelli resigned amid complaints about his heavy-handed management and whether his pay package of $123.7 million (excluding [[stock option]] grants) over the previous five years was excessive, considering the stock's poor performance versus its competitor [[Lowe's]]. His [[severance package]] of $210 million was criticized because when the stock went down, his pay went up.<ref name="Corporate news release"/><ref name="Business Week article">{{cite web | url=http://www.businessweek.com/stories/2007-01-04/home-depots-surprising-choice-for-ceobusinessweek-business-news-stock-market-and-financial-advice| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121004013625/http://www.businessweek.com/stories/2007-01-04/home-depots-surprising-choice-for-ceobusinessweek-business-news-stock-market-and-financial-advice| archive-date=October 4, 2012| work= [[Bloomberg Businessweek|BusinessWeek]]| title=Home Depot's Surprising Choice for CEO| date=January 4, 2007| access-date=October 16, 2022}}</ref>

His successor, [[Frank Blake (businessman)|Frank Blake]], previously served as the company's vice chairman of the board and executive vice president. Blake agreed to a much more conservative compensation package than Nardelli, which is very heavily dependent upon the success of the company. Although a longtime deputy to Nardelli at GE and Home Depot, Blake was said to lack Nardelli's hard edge and instead preferred to make decisions by consensus. Indeed, Blake repudiated many of his predecessor's strategies, and it has been reported that the two men have not spoken since Nardelli departed Home Depot.<ref name="Corporate news release">{{cite web | url=http://ir.homedepot.com/phoenix.zhtml?c=63646&p=irol-newsArticle_Print&ID=1267184| publisher=The Home Depot| title=Robert Nardelli Resigns as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of The Home Depot and Is Succeeded by Frank Blake| work=News Releases| date=January 3, 2007| access-date=January 19, 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160123220127/http://ir.homedepot.com/phoenix.zhtml?c=63646&p=irol-newsArticle_Print&ID=1267184| archive-date=January 23, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Business Week article"/>

In 2008 and 2009, with the downturn in the housing market, The Home Depot announced the layoff of several thousand associates, as well as the closing of 54 stores nationwide, including the entire EXPO Design Center chain.<ref>{{cite web | author=Meg Marco| url=https://consumerist.com/2009/01/26/bid-adieu-to-home-depots-expo-stores/#:~:text=Home%20Depot%20said%20on%20Wednesday,professional%20building%20and%20repair%20market.| title=Bid Adieu To Home Depot's Expo Stores| work=Consumerist | publisher=Consumerist.com| date=January 26, 2009| access-date=October 16, 2022}}</ref> Associates at EXPO were allowed to re-apply for Home Depot jobs after the [[layoff]]s, and did not lose any tenure if hired back. In the year of February 2009, sales totaled $71.288 billion, more than $20 billion down from the peak of two years earlier due to the sale of HD Supply and falling revenue at the retained business. In 2012, it proceeded to close the big-box style stores that it had in China, however, smaller stores that specialized in custom products and that focused on more intimate interactions between customers and associates remain open there.<ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.ft.com/content/5d69bbb0-fe13-11e1-8fc3-00144feabdc0| title=Home Depot shuts big box stores in China| last=Jopson| first=Barney| date=September 14, 2012| work=[[Financial Times]]}}</ref> In 2013, The Home Depot established two large distribution centers in [[Atlanta]] and [[Los Angeles]].<ref>{{cite news | title=Home Depot to build two distribution centers to expand online fulfillment network| last=Solomon| first=Mark B| url=https://www.dcvelocity.com/articles/26358-home-depot-to-build-two-distribution-centers-to-expand-online-fulfillment-network| access-date=October 16, 2022| publisher=DC Velocity| date=March 22, 2013}}</ref>

[[File:InterlinebrandsJacksonville.jpg|thumb|upright|Interline Brands headquarters in [[Jacksonville, Florida]], 2016 ]]

In August 2014, it was announced that Frank Blake would step down as CEO and would be replaced by 57-year-old [[Craig Menear]]. The change occurred on November 1, 2014. Blake continued with the company as chairman. Menear joined The Home Depot in 1997 and served in various management and vice-presidential positions, until 2003, including merchandising vice president of hardware, merchandising vice president of the Southwest Division, and divisional merchandise manager of the Southwest Division. He subsequently served as senior vice president of merchandising from August 2003 to April 2007. He then served as an executive vice president of merchandising from April 2007 to February 2014. Until becoming CEO, Menear served as president of U.S. Retail from February 2014 to November 1, 2014.<ref>{{cite magazine | url=https://www.bloomberg.com/research/stocks/people/person.asp?personId=6611970&ticker=HD| title=Executive Profile Craig A. Menear| magazine=[[Bloomberg Business]]}}</ref>

The company had a data breach in September 2014.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-home-depot-dataprotection-breach-prob/connecticut-illinois-california-lead-probe-into-home-depot-data-breach-idUSKBN0H41SC20140909| title=Connecticut, Illinois, California lead probe into Home Depot data breach| work=[[Reuters]]| date=September 9, 2014| access-date=October 16, 2022}}</ref> One major reason for the data breach was the practice of entering credit card numbers directly into computers at the service-desk and pro-desk, and in specialty departments including flooring, kitchen cabinets, appliances, and [[Millwork (building material)|millwork]], rather than using POS credit card terminals directly. The practice was stopped, and Home Depot offered a year of free credit monitoring through AllClearID for any customers who requested it. There were also reports of credit card numbers being stolen when used to make purchases on Homedepot.com.

On July 22, 2015, Home Depot announced it would acquire [[Interline Brands]] from P2 Capital Partners, [[Goldman Sachs|Goldman Sachs']] private equity arm, and the management of Interline Brands for $1.6 billion.<ref>{{cite news | last=Bray| first=Chad| title=Home Depot to Buy Interline Brands for $1.6 Billion in Cash| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/07/23/business/dealbook/home-depot-to-buy-interline-brands-for-1-6-billion-in-cash.html| access-date=October 16, 2022| newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| date=July 22, 2015}}</ref> On August 24, 2015, The Home Depot completed its acquisition of Interline Brands. By August 2016, the integration was progressing, with Interline's products being piloted in 20 Home Depot stores and its website merging with Home Depot's platform.<ref>{{cite news | title=How Interline, Home Depot are becoming 'one'| url=https://www.bizjournals.com/jacksonville/news/2016/07/18/behind-the-scenes-of-the-interline-home-depot-deal.html| access-date=April 26, 2017| newspaper=Jacksonville Business Journal| date=July 18, 2016}}</ref>

In 2017, Home Depot acquired the online presence of The Company Store from [[Hanover Direct]]. The Company Store was founded in 1911, operating primarily as a catalog and online sales operation, but with five physical locations. The five physical locations were not included in the deal.<ref>{{cite web | last=Howland| first=Daphne| url=https://www.retaildive.com/news/home-depot-buys-the-company-store/513732/| title=Home Depot Buys The Company Store| website=RetailDive| date=December 22, 2017| access-date=October 16, 2022}}</ref> In December 2020, Home Depot bought back HD Supply for $8 billion.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-12-29 |title=The Home Depot Completes $8B HD Supply Acquisition |url=https://www.inddist.com/mergers-acquisitions/news/21219374/the-home-depot-completes-8b-hd-supply-acquisition |access-date=2024-06-01 |website=Industrial Distribution |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Home Depot buys back HD Supply in $8B deal |url=https://www.retaildive.com/news/home-depot-buys-back-hd-supply-in-8b-deal/589109/ |access-date=2024-06-01 |website=Retail Dive |language=en-US}}</ref> In January 2022, The Home Depot announced Craig Menear would be stepping down as the CEO and president effective March 1, 2022, while continuing to serve as the chairman of the board. He was replaced by former executive vice president [[Ted Decker]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://corporate.homedepot.com/newsroom/teddecker-named-ceo| title=The Home Depot Names Ted Decker CEO, Effective March 1, 2022; Craig Menear Continues as Chair of the Board| publisher=The Home Depot| date=January 27, 2022| access-date=October 16, 2022}}</ref>

In February 2023, Home Depot announced that it would spend $1 billion to raise hourly employee wages.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Repko |first=Melissa |title=Home Depot says it will spend $1 billion to give hourly workers a raise |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/02/21/home-depot-hourly-workers-raise.html |access-date=2023-03-21 |website=[[CNBC]] |date=February 21, 2023 |language=en}}</ref> On March 28, 2024 the company announced it would acquire SRS Distribution for $18.25 billion; SRS is based in [[McKinney, Texas]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mdm.com/news/top-distributor-sectors/building-materials-construction/home-depot-completes-18-billion-purchase-of-srs-distribution|title=Home Depot Completes $18 Billion Purchase of SRS Distribution|last=Hockett|first=Mike|date=June 18, 2024|access-date=August 28, 2025|work=MDM (Modern Distribution Management)}}</ref> In turn, Home Depot agreed to buy Gypsum Management & Supply, Inc. (GMS) of [[Tucker, Georgia]] in late June 2025 for approximately $4.3 billion.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wahba |first=Phil |title=Home Depot's $5 billion purchase of an unsexy building products distributor is a prime example of smart M&A |url=https://fortune.com/2025/07/01/home-depot-gms-deal-stock-outlook/ |access-date=2025-09-05 |website=Fortune |language=en}}</ref> The acquisition was finalized in September 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Battle |first=Patricia |date=2025-09-08 |title=Home Depot seals billion-dollar acquisition to win back shoppers |url=https://www.thestreet.com/retail/home-depot-seals-billion-dollar-acquisition-to-win-back-shoppers |access-date=2025-09-08 |website=TheStreet |language=en-us}}</ref> In March 2026, SRS Distribution acquired Mingledorff's Inc., a wholesale distributor of [[heating, ventilation, and air conditioning]] equipment, parts and supplies, with 42 locations in five states across the Southeastern U.S. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed.<ref name=csa>{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Marianne |date=2026-03-24|title=Home Depot subsidiary SRS Distribution to acquire HVAC wholesaler  |url=https://chainstoreage.com/home-depot-subsidiary-srs-distribution-acquire-hvac-wholesaler|access-date=2026-04-13|website=Chain Store Age |language=en}}</ref>

In March 2026, SRS Distribution, a subsidiary of Home Depot, agreed to acquire Mingledorff's Inc., a wholesale distributor of heating, ventilation, and air conditioning equipment, parts and supplies, operating 42 locations across five southeastern states. The acquisition completed in May 2026, expanding SRS into the HVAC distribution market.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SRS Distribution Completes Acquisition of HVAC Distributor Mingledorff's |url=https://ir.homedepot.com/news-releases/2026/05-11-2026-133053552 |access-date=2026-08-31 |website=ir.homedepot.com |language=en}}</ref>

In July 2026, Home Depot announced an organizational realignment focused on expanding its professional-customer business. The company renamed its Office of integration as the Office of Pro Acceleration, led by chief financial officer Richard McPhail, to coordinate operations across Home Depot Pro, HD Supply, SRS Distribution, and Construction resources.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Home Depot Announces Organizational Realignment to Provide a More Seamless Customer Experience, Drive Growth and Capture Market Share |url=https://ir.homedepot.com/news-releases/2026/07-30-2026-210819756 |access-date=2026-08-31 |website=ir.homedepot.com |language=en}}</ref>

As of 2020, Home Depot is ranked No. 26 on the [[Fortune 500]] rankings of the largest United States corporations by total revenue.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://fortune.com/fortune500/list/|title=Fortune 500 Companies 2018: Who Made the List|website=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]]|language=en-US|access-date=November 9, 2018|archive-date=January 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190115060417/http://fortune.com/fortune500/list/}}</ref> In 2023, the company was ranked 67th in the [[Forbes Global 2000]].<ref>{{Cite web|language=en|url=https://www.forbes.com/lists/global2000/?sh=51d599675ac0|title=The Global 2000 2023|website=Forbes|access-date=2024-02-07|archive-date=2024-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240129031905/https://www.forbes.com/lists/global2000/?sh=4f5ab07e5ac0}}</ref>

For the Q2 of 2020, the company reported sales of $38.1 billion, which represented a growth of 23.4% from the same period, the previous year. The net earnings for the period of three months (ending August 2) rose 27% up to $4.3 billion. The growth in the sales was a result of Americans staying at home as a result of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/35edd003-63e0-4aec-b786-bd7733b0530d|title= Home Depot sales soar as Americans turn to DIY|work=[[Financial Times]]|last=Provan|first=Sarah|date=August 18, 2020|access-date=August 18, 2020}}</ref> In the Q3 for 2020, ending November 1, Home Depot reported a revenue of $33.5 billion; it represents a year-on-year increase of 24 per cent.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/ed02767c-48cd-418f-baa9-49cd44ed5310|title= Walmart and Home Depot extend pandemic winning streaks |work=[[Financial Times]]|author=Alistair Gray|date=November 17, 2020|access-date=November 17, 2020}}</ref>

==Mascot==
[[File:Home Depot Rental Van.jpg|thumb|upright=1|Home Depot rental [[Ford Transit]] in [[Oshawa]], [[Ontario]]]]

The Home Depot's mascot has been Homer D. Poe since 1981 when he was first used in advertising. Gwyn Raker, the illustrator, says, "I designed him to be a funny guy next door who wasn't intimidating." The Homer Fund, a for-associate charity, is named after the mascot, who since its creation, has been a part of Home Depot culture ever since. This includes signage, advertising, awards, and even a life-size costume for stores to rent out. Homer has a wife, named Daisy, and a dog, named Carl.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://corporate.homedepot.com/newsroom/meet-homer-home-depots-much-loved-diy-mascot|title=Meet Homer: The Home Depot's Much-Loved DIY Mascot|date=January 23, 2015|work=The Home Depot|access-date=December 10, 2017|language=en}}</ref>

==Operation==
Home Depot stores average 105,000&nbsp;ft<sup>2</sup> (9,755 m<sup>2</sup>) in size and are organized warehouse-style, stocking a large range of supplies. Home Depot's two largest stores are located in [[Vauxhall, New Jersey]], which encompasses 217,000&nbsp;ft<sup>2</sup> of space, and in [[Anaheim Hills, California]], where it encompasses 204,000&nbsp;ft<sup>2</sup>.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ocregister.com/articles/home-347749-store-new.html|title=The Home Depot opens its first Superstore in the West|work=The Orange County Register|date=April 5, 2012|access-date=September 21, 2014}}</ref> The company color is a bright orange (PMS 165, CMYK 60M100Y, HEX FF6600), on signs, equipment and employee aprons.<ref>{{cite magazine|last1=Sharf|first1=Samantha|title=Home Depot Announces New CEO, Frank Blake To Stay On As Chairman|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/samanthasharf/2014/08/21/home-depot-announces-new-ceo-frank-blake-to-stay-on-as-chairman/|magazine=Forbes|access-date=August 22, 2014}}</ref>

===Contractors===
Contractors make up only  five percent of Home Depot's customers but they account for 45 percent of the company's $132 billion in annual sales. To address these contractor customers the company is building new flatbed distribution centers designed specifically to cater to builders that roll up in a contractor [[flatbed truck]]s.<ref>{{cite news |last=Holman |first=Jordyn |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-12-02/home-depot-seeks-to-win-over-lucrative-pro-clients-with-new-hubs |title=Home Depot Is Spending Big to Keep Lucrative Contractors Happy |work=[[Bloomberg News]] |date=2021-12-02 |access-date=2021-12-06 }}</ref>

===Marketing===
The Home Depot announced the new slogan "How Doers Get More Done" on December 5, 2019, replacing the previous slogan "More saving. More doing." which was introduced in the March 18, 2009, circular, replacing "You can do it. We can help." which had been used since 2003.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.corporate-eye.com/main/home-depot-gets-a-slogan-makeover/|title=Home Depot Gets a Slogan Makeover|website=www.corporate-eye.com|date=April 10, 2009 |language=en-US|access-date=April 26, 2017}}</ref> Other slogans used in the past 25 years include "The Home Depot, Low prices are just the beginning" in the early 1990s and "When you're at the Home Depot, You'll feel right at home" in the late 1990s and "The Home Depot: First In Home Improvement!" from 1999 to 2003.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.protoolreviews.com/news/home-depot-2009-slogan/2738/|title=Home Depot Slogan {{!}} Pro Tool Reviews|date=March 24, 2009|work=Pro Tool Reviews|access-date=December 27, 2017|language=en-US}}</ref>

===U.S. Stores division===
[[File:Home Depot locations.png|thumb|Home Depot locations]]
Long-time employee Marc Powers became the head of Home Depot's U.S. stores division in 2014. He took the place of Marvin Ellison, who left to become the chief executive of [[J.C. Penney]]. In January 2016, Home Depot announced the departure of Powers as division head, to be replaced by another veteran employee, [[Ann-Marie Campbell]], one of Powers' deputies. The change in leadership is effective as of February 1, 2016. Ms. Campbell has been employed by Home Depot for over 30 years, beginning as a cashier in a branch in [[South Florida]]. Her most recent role was as president of Home Depot's Southern division.<ref name="Wall Street Journal-Home Depot Replaces Head of U.S. Stores Business">{{cite news|last1=Ziobro|first1=Paul|title=Home Depot Replaces Head of U.S. Stores Business|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/home-depot-replaces-head-of-u-s-stores-business-1453239562|newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|access-date=January 21, 2016|date=January 19, 2016}}</ref>

===Distribution centers===
[[File:The Home Depot RDC 5085.JPG|thumb|upright=1|The Home Depot distribution center in [[Lake Park, Georgia]]]]

The Home Depot has over 90 distribution centers throughout the United States to serve over 2,000 The Home Depot stores.<ref>{{cite web|title=Operations|url=https://corporate.homedepot.com/responsibility/operations|website=The Home Depot|date=February 28, 2016|access-date=April 22, 2017}}</ref>

===Online===
The domain ''homedepot.com'' attracted at least 120 million visitors annually by 2008 according to a [[Compete.com]] survey.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://siteanalytics.compete.com/homedepot.com?metric=uv|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110813045523/http://siteanalytics.compete.com/homedepot.com/?metric=uv|archive-date=August 13, 2011|title=homedepot.com UVs for March 2012|publisher=Compete|access-date=April 29, 2012}}</ref> In the US HomeDepot.com has 5 Call centers located in Kennesaw, GA; Atlanta, GA; Marietta, GA; Ogden, UT; and Tempe, AZ. Home Depot online offers [[Online shopping#Product delivery|in-store pickup]] and online returns.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/home-depot-vs-lowes-compared-pictures-details-2018-4#this-store-offers-same-day-delivery-anywhere-in-manhattan-starting-at-21-other-home-depot-locations-also-do-this-with-prices-varying-based-on-the-order-size-18|title=We shopped at Home Depot and Lowe's to see which store was better – and the winner was clear for one key reason|work=[[Business Insider]]|access-date=April 14, 2018}}</ref>{{Better source needed|date=March 2021}}

===Fuel centers===
In 2006, The Home Depot began testing [[gasoline station|fuel center]]s at some of its stores. The first two "Home Depot Fuel" convenience stores (C-Store) were located in [[Tennessee]]. Four additional prototype stores were built in [[Acworth, Georgia]]; [[Smyrna, Tennessee]]; [[Greensboro, Georgia]]; and [[Winchester, Tennessee]].<ref name="The Home Depot Opens First Home Depot Fuel Location in Georgia">{{cite web|url=http://ir.homedepot.com/ReleaseDetail.cfm?ReleaseID=212065|publisher=PR Newswire|title=The Home Depot Opens First Home Depot Fuel Location in Georgia|date=September 25, 2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061101014043/http://ir.homedepot.com/ReleaseDetail.cfm?ReleaseID=212065|archive-date=November 1, 2006}}</ref> In 2012, Home Depot VP of Corporate Communication Stephen Holmes said that the company had no plans for additional fuel centers or growth in that area.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://csnews.com/whatever-happened-home-depot-fuel|title=Whatever Happened to Home Depot Fuel?|website=Convenience Store News|date=June 27, 2012 |language=en|access-date=March 29, 2019}}</ref>

===Tool, vehicle and equipment rental===
The Home Depot offers tool, vehicle, and equipment rentals at most of its locations.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tool and Vehicle Rental |url=https://www.homedepot.ca/en/home/tool-and-vehicle-rental.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220809145200/https://www.homedepot.ca/en/home/tool-and-vehicle-rental.html |archive-date=August 9, 2022 |access-date=August 9, 2022 |website=The Home Depot}}</ref> Truck and van options include [[flatbed truck]]s, [[Van|cargo vans]], and [[box truck]]s in various sizes. Professional-quality construction, landscaping, and household equipment, ranging from hand tools to large machinery, are available. Rentals are offered in 4-hour, daily, weekly, and monthly terms.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tool Rental FAQs & Policies |url=https://www.homedepot.com/c/Tool_Rental_FAQ |access-date=2025-07-21 |website=The Home Depot |language=en}}</ref>

==Subsidiaries and private brands==
===Wholly owned subsidiaries===

====Blinds.com====
{{anchor|Blinds.com}}
[[File:Blindscom-logo-300x59.png|left|thumb|upright=.8]]

Blinds.com is an [[e-commerce]] retailer of [[window blinds]] and [[window covering]]s.<ref>[http://www.bizjournals.com/houston/print-edition/2014/01/31/deal-of-the-weekhouston-online-blinds-retailer.html ''Deal of the Week: Houston online blinds retailer scooped up by national powerhouse'']; Ryan, Molly, Houston Business Journal; 2014-01-31</ref> Blinds.com was founded by [[Jay Steinfeld]] in 1993.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jay Steinfeld - About |url=https://www.jaysteinfeld.com/about |access-date=2022-10-22 |website=www.jaysteinfeld.com |language=en}}</ref> By 2006, the company was named No. 186 on the Internet Retailer Top 500 Guide, as well as the 10th fastest-growing e-commerce company on the list.<ref>[http://www.chron.com/business/article/Houston-s-Blinds-com-prospers-on-Web-1514945.php ''Houston's Blinds.com prospers on Web'']; Kaplan, David; Houston Chronicle; 2006-07-08</ref> In 2009, Blinds.com was given the Marketer of the Year Award by the [[American Marketing Association]], in recognition of its innovative marketing strategy.<ref>{{cite web | last=| first=| date=| title=Blinds.com Named 2009 Marketer of the Year &#124; AMA Houston| url=http://amahouston.net/blinds-com-named-2009-marketer-of-the-year/| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140811165054/http://amahouston.net/blinds-com-named-2009-marketer-of-the-year/| archive-date=2014-08-11| access-date=2014-07-29| website=}} Subramanian, Shanthi, "Blinds.com Named 2009 Marketer of the Year".  AMA Houston website.  2010-03-18.</ref> In response to demand for window coverings that could be installed quickly and easily, CMO Daniel Cotlar led a partnership with a manufacturing vendor to design a window shade that could be installed without tools or adhesive.  This led to the company's patent-pending Instafit shade product.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://appft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&p=1&u=/netahtml/PTO/search-adv.html&r=1&f=G&l=50&d=PG01&S1=20140086676&OS=20140086676&RS=20140086676 |title=United States Patent Application: 0140086676 |website=appft.uspto.gov |access-date=26 January 2022}}</ref> In January 2014, Blinds.com was acquired by The Home Depot.<ref>[https://www.wsj.com/article/BT-CO-20140123-712620.html Kell, John, ''Home Depot Acquires Blinds.com'']; Wall Street Journal.  2014-01-23</ref>

====Compact Power Equipment Inc.====
Compact Power Equipment Inc. was a power equipment rental company that prior to 2017 provided equipment to rental departments in over 1,000 Home Depots in North America. It was acquired by The Home Depot on July 6, 2017.<ref name="invst">[https://www.investopedia.com/articles/company-insights/082416/top-7-companies-owned-home-depot-hd.asp ''6 Companies Owned by Home Depot'']; Reiff, Nathan; 09 July 2021; article; Investopedia; on-line; accessed October 2022</ref>

====The Home Depot Pro====
[[File:InterlinebrandsJAX16.jpg|thumb|upright=1|Interline Brands distribution center in [[Jacksonville, Florida]]]]

The Home Depot Pro (known until 2018 as '''Interline Brands''') has over 90 distribution centers throughout the United States, Canada, and Puerto Rico that serve customer needs for [[Maintenance, repair, and operations|MRO]] supplies.<ref name="invst" /><ref>{{cite news | title=Home Depot to acquire Interline Brands| url=http://www.industrialsupplymagazine.com/pages/News-072215-Home-Depot-to-acquire-Interline-Brands.php| access-date=October 13, 2016| publisher=Industrial Supply| date=July 22, 2015}}</ref>

Brands of the division include:
* Wilmar Industries (MRO)
* Barnett (MRO, contractor supplies)
* Maintenance USA (MRO)
* SupplyWorks (janitorial, packaging, MRO)
* US Lock (keys, security devices)
* Hardware Express (hardware supplies)
* {{not a typo|Leran}} Gas Products (propane accessories)

====The Company Store ====
[[File:HomeDepotPickupLockers.jpg|thumb|Home Depot online order pickup lockers]]

Online seller of textile and textile goods for the home decor market. Originally founded in 1911 as a purveyor of home furnishings, its online division—only—was acquired by THD in 2017.<ref name="invst" />

====Redbeacon====
Online contractor referral service founded in 2009; now called THD Pro Referral.<ref name="invst" />

====HD Supply ====
{{Main|HD Supply}}

HD Supply is an industrial supply and distribution company. The company, formerly called The Maintenance Warehouse, provided infrastructure and construction support services for businesses throughout North America.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://fortune.com/fortune500/hd-supply-holdings/| title=HD Supply Holdings| website=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]]| access-date=2018-12-28}}</ref> Renamed as HD Supply, the business was re-acquired by THD in December 2020.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bizjournals.com/atlanta/news/2020/12/24/home-depot-buys-competitor-hd-supply.html |title=Home Depot completes $8 billion purchase of HD Supply |date=December 24, 2020 |first=Eric |last=Mandel |publisher=Atlanta Business Chronicle}}</ref><ref name="invst" />

====USABlueBook ====
Providing equipment, chemicals, and laboratory supplies to municipal and industrial water professionals. Their "Master Catalog" is a staple in the industry, featuring over 57,000 items. USABlueBook is the leading distributor of Maintenance, Repair, and Operations (MRO) supplies for the water and wastewater treatment industry.<ref>{{Cite web |title=About USABlueBook |url=https://www.usabluebook.com/resources/about |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=USABlueBook}}</ref>
