===Philanthropy===
The Home Depot Foundation is the philanthropic arm of the company created in 2002. It has contributed over $200 million in time, labor, money, and supplies to a number of causes, including [[Habitat for Humanity]], California-based [[City of Hope National Medical Center]], and playground construction organization KaBOOM!<ref>{{cite web|title=Business & Industry: The Home Depot|author=Bailey, M.|publisher=Georgia College and State University|url=http://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/nge/Article.jsp?id=h-1886&sug=y}}</ref> Home Depot supports the U.S. Military community with a 10% military discount. Since 1993, the "Team Depot" program has provided grants to veteran-based organizations and has workers from a local store do volunteer work that would benefit veterans.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.themorningsun.com/news/local/mt-pleasant-american-legion-building-gets-improved-by-volunteers/article_11cb6dda-d886-11e8-b3a9-d7365f0f0ae7.html|title=Mt. Pleasant American Legion building gets improved by volunteers|first=Cory|last=Micho|work=The Morning Sun|location=[[Mount Pleasant, Michigan]]|date=October 25, 2018|access-date=October 1, 2018}}</ref>

The Home Depot has partnered with the [[Georgia Emergency Management Agency]]'s [[Ready Georgia]] campaign, leading both supplies and facility use to this statewide effort to increase emergency preparedness among Georgia's children.<ref>{{citation|title=The Home Depot Partners with GEMA's Ready Georgia to Teach Thousands of Kids about Emergency Preparedness|url=http://www.fayettefrontpage.com/public-safety/09/8-10-09_home-depot-gema.html|publisher=The Fayette Front Page|date=August 10, 2009|access-date=November 10, 2009|archive-date=December 9, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241209094427/http://www.fayettefrontpage.com/public-safety/09/8-10-09_home-depot-gema.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> The company also provided [[survival kit|ready kits]] and other prizes for an art and essay contest for Georgia elementary school students.<ref>Ready Georgia, ''Congratulations to our 'Get Ready Georgia' Art and Essay Contest Winners!'' Retrieved November 3, 2009.</ref>

In March 2018, the company donated $50 million to train 20,000 people as construction workers over the next decade. The Home Builders Institute will use the money to train veterans and [[United States Army|U.S. Army]] soldiers, high school students, and disadvantaged youth. The financial support from Home Depot was to help address the needs of the shortage of construction workers.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2018/03/08/exclusive-home-depot-donate-50-m-train-construction-workers-address-severe-shortage/403659002/|title=Exclusive: Home Depot to donate $50M to train construction workers, address severe shortage|work=USA Today|access-date=April 30, 2018|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.marketplace.org/2018/04/30/economy/home-depot-takes-shot-tackling-construction-labor-shortage|title=Home Depot takes a shot at tackling the construction labor shortage|access-date=April 30, 2018}}</ref>

===Environmental record===
On their website the company says they have a commitment to "continue to lead by example, demonstrating to the world that sustainability business practices are not only possible, they are good for business."<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.treehugger.com/corporate-responsibility/home-depot-giving-going-green-strategies.html|title=Is Home Depot giving up on "Going Green" Strategies?|work=TreeHugger|access-date=April 7, 2017}}</ref> The Home Depot introduced a label on nearly 3,000 products in 2007. The label promotes energy conservation, sustainable forestry, and clean water. Home Depot executives said that as the world's largest buyer of construction material, their company had the power to persuade thousands of suppliers, homebuilders, and consumers to follow its lead on environment sustainability. "Who in the world has a chance to have a bigger impact on this sector than Home Depot?" asked Ron Jarvis, vice president for environmental innovation at Home Depot.<ref name="EnvLabel">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/04/17/business/17depot.html|work=[[The New York Times]] |title=Home Depot to Display an Environmental Label|date=April 17, 2007 | first=Michael | last=Barbaro | access-date=May 25, 2010}}</ref> This program is following The Home Depot's promise in the late 1990s to eliminate the number of sales of lumber from endangered forests in countries including Chile and Indonesia.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.planetark.org/dailynewsstory.cfm/newsid/19281/story.htm|publisher=Planet ARK|title=Home Depot adopts new wood purchasing policy|date=January 6, 2003|access-date=May 6, 2008|archive-date=March 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306062621/http://planetark.org/dailynewsstory.cfm/newsid/19281/story.htm}}</ref>

Additionally, The Home Depot promotes recycling [[compact fluorescent]] light bulbs in its stores. As part of this effort, the company created the largest [[recycling]] program in the United States for the bulbs.<ref name="CFL Recycling" >{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/06/24/business/24recycling.html|work=[[The New York Times]]|title=Home Depot Offers Recycling for Compact Fluorescent Bulbs|date=June 24, 2008|first=Stephanie|last=Rosenbloom|access-date=May 25, 2010}}</ref>
In March 2013, Home Depot locations in Canada stopped accepting compact fluorescent light bulbs for recycling.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/ottawa/home-depot-quietly-ends-light-bulb-recycling-program-1.1314273 |title=Home Depot quietly ends light-bulb-recycling program |publisher=Cbc.ca}}</ref>

===Television===
In 2002, The Home Depot joined PBS as a sponsor of ''[[This Old House]]'' and ''[[Ask This Old House]]''. In 2003, The Home Depot became a sponsor for ''[[Trading Spaces]]''.

===Sports===
Company co-founder Arthur Blank purchased the [[Atlanta Falcons]] franchise of the [[National Football League]] in February 2002; Blank later acquired an expansion franchise in [[Major League Soccer]], [[Atlanta United FC]], in April 2014 with the soccer club beginning play in March 2017. The Home Depot made no formal association with the Falcons until April 2017, when The Home Depot acquired the naming rights to the {{convert|11|acre|m2|-1|adj=on}} park adjacent to [[Mercedes-Benz Stadium]]. The Home Depot Backyard occupies the site of the former [[Georgia Dome]], and serves as parking and tailgating space during Falcons' and Atlanta United FC home games and public use greenspace during non-event days. The park opened on September 11, 2018.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Stafford|first1=Leon|title=Georgia Dome site to become park after demolition|url=http://www.ajc.com/news/local-govt--politics/georgia-dome-site-become-park-after-demolition/m3MUfdcQPNgkXCujCsvwJJ/|access-date=April 26, 2017|work=The Atlanta Journal-Constitution|date=April 21, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Home Depot Backyard opens at Mercedes-Benz Stadium |date=September 12, 2018 |url=http://www.fox5atlanta.com/local-news/home-depot-backyard-opens-at-mercedes-benz-stadium#/ |publisher=WAGA-TV |access-date=September 12, 2018}}</ref> The Home Depot was a sponsor of the [[2026 FIFA World Cup]], which took place in the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

[[File:Home Depot Center entrance.jpg|thumb|From 2003 to 2013 [[Dignity Health Sports Park]] was known as The Home Depot Center]]

Since 1991, the company has become a large supporter of athletics, sponsoring the [[United States Olympic Committee|United States]] and [[Canadian Olympic Committee|Canadian Olympic team]]s, and launching a program which offered employment to athletes that accommodates their training and competition schedules. The Home Depot ceased to be a sponsor of the Canadian Olympic Team in 2005 and ended a sponsorship program for the United States Olympic team in 2009.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-homedepot-olympics/home-depot-ends-olympics-sponsorship-program-idUSTRE5076X120090108|title=Home Depot ends Olympics sponsorship program|date=January 8, 2009|work=[[Reuters]]|access-date=March 2, 2018}}</ref>

The Home Depot was a major sponsor for [[Joe Gibbs Racing]] in [[NASCAR]] from 1999 to 2014. Their arrival into the series coincided with [[Tony Stewart]] leaving the [[Indy Racing League]] to join the [[NASCAR Cup Series]]. Stewart drove The Home Depot-sponsored No. 20 car for Joe Gibbs Racing until 2008, winning 2 of his 3 series championships in the car, and was succeeded by [[Joey Logano]], who took the car to victory lane twice. After [[Matt Kenseth]] joined the team, The Home Depot's status as the No. 20's primary sponsor was taken over by [[Dollar General]], but the company still served as its most frequent secondary sponsor through its Husky Tools division. On June 23, 2014, the company announced it would end its NASCAR sponsorship after 2014.<ref>{{cite web|last=Pennell|first=Jay|url=http://msn.foxsports.com/nascar/story/report-home-depot-ending-nascar-sponsorship-after-2014-062314|title=Report: Home Depot ending NASCAR sponsorship after 2014|work=[[Foxsports.com]]|date=June 23, 2014|access-date=June 23, 2014}}</ref>

[[File:2009-0912-GameDay-FowlerHoward.jpg|thumb|right|[[College GameDay (football)|ESPN College GameDay]] has been sponsored by The Home Depot since 2007.]]

The Home Depot was the title sponsor of The Home Depot Center in [[Carson, California]], home to the [[Los Angeles Galaxy]] of Major League Soccer; the venue was formerly the home of [[Chivas USA]] of MLS, which folded in 2014, and the [[Los Angeles Riptide]] of [[Major League Lacrosse]], which folded in 2008. The venue is now called [[Dignity Health Sports Park]].

In 2006, The Home Depot partnered with [[Duke University]]'s [[Edmund T. Pratt Jr. School of Engineering]] to create "The Home Depot Smart Home". The smart home is a live-in laboratory for ten upper-class engineering students that allows them to immerse themselves in the work. The goal of the project is to help provide innovative solutions for the home in areas such as security and home monitoring, communications, energy efficiency, entertainment, environment, and health.<ref name="The Home Depot Smart Home">{{cite news|url=http://today.duke.edu/2006/10/smarthome.html|publisher=[[Duke University]]|title=Duke Announces Construction of 'The Home Depot Smart Home'|date=October 24, 2006}}</ref> In January 2007, The Home Depot became the official home improvement sponsor of ESPN's College Gameday.<ref name="NFL sponsorship">{{cite web|url=http://ir.homedepot.com/releasedetail.cfm?releaseid=224939|publisher=The Home Depot|title=The Home Depot Becomes an Official NFL Sponsor|date=January 9, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070121174052/http://ir.homedepot.com/ReleaseDetail.cfm?ReleaseID=224939|archive-date=January 21, 2007}}</ref>

===Politics===
Seventy-three percent of The Home Depot's campaign contributions went to [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] candidates in the [[United States general elections, 2006|2005–2006 US elections]]. "Home Depot's PAC gives money based on a candidate's voting record, committee assignment and leadership position," said company spokesman Jerry Shields.<ref name="Bloomberg News">{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601103&sid=ax33MvEtvy0E&refer=news|publisher=[[Bloomberg L.P.|Bloomberg]]|title=Republican Candidates Increase Share of Business PAC Donations|date=August 8, 2006}}</ref> The CEO in this period was [[Bob Nardelli]], a friend of U.S. President [[George W. Bush]].<ref name="AP">{{Cite news|url=https://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_qn4188/is_20070103/ai_n17090979/print|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080317043833/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_qn4188/is_20070103/ai_n17090979/print|url-status=usurped|archive-date=March 17, 2008|publisher=AP.com|title=Nardelli resigns abruptly as CEO of Home Depot, leaves with $210M|date=January 3, 2007|first=Harry R.|last=Weber}}</ref>  Nardelli hosted a garden reception/fundraiser for Bush at his Atlanta home on May 20, 2004.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2004/may/23/usa.uselections2004|title=Bush's Super Fundraisers Join the Queue for Favours|first=Paul|last=Harris|date=May 23, 2004|access-date=October 24, 2007|work= [[The Guardian]]}}</ref>

In 2005, The Home Depot was among 53 entities that contributed the maximum of $250,000 to the second inauguration of President [[George W. Bush]].<ref>{{Cite news|first=Jim |last=Drinkard|title=Donors Get Good Seats, Great Access This Week |url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/washington/2005-01-16-inauguration-donors_x.htm |work=[[USA Today]]|date=January 17, 2005|access-date=August 22, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=<!--Not stated-->|title=Financing the Inauguration |url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/washington/2005-01-16-inaugural-donors_x.htm |work= [[USA Today]]|date=January 16, 2005|access-date=August 22, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=<!--Not stated-->|title=Some Question Inaugural's Multi-Million Price Tag |url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/washington/2005-01-14-price_x.htm|publisher= Associated Press (via [[USA Today]])|date=January 14, 2005|access-date= August 22, 2012}}</ref> According to the [[Watchdog journalism|watchdog group]] Documented, in 2020, The Home Depot contributed $125,000 to the Rule of Law Defense Fund, a fundraising arm of the [[Republican Attorneys General Association]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://documented.net/2021/01/republican-attorneys-general-dark-money-group-organized-protest-preceding-capitol-mob-attack/|title=Republican Attorneys General Dark Money Group Organized Protest Preceding Capitol Attack|date=January 7, 2021|access-date=January 11, 2021|publisher=Documented|first=Jamie|last=Corey}}</ref>

In April 2021, Black faith leaders in Georgia called for a nationwide boycott of The Home Depot after the company did not take a stand against the [[Election Integrity Act of 2021]].<ref>{{cite web|date=April 20, 2021|title=Church leaders call for Home Depot boycott over Georgia voting curbs|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/home-depot-face-boycott-over-georgia-voting-curbs-2021-04-20/|access-date=April 20, 2021|website=[[Reuters]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Georgia religious leaders call for boycott of Home Depot over silence on voting laws|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/georgia-religious-leaders-call-boycott-home-depot-over-silence-voting-n1264674|access-date=April 20, 2021|website=[[NBC News]]|date=April 20, 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Corasaniti|first=Nick|date=April 20, 2021|title=Georgia Faith Leaders Urge Boycott of Home Depot Over Voting Law|language=en-US|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/20/us/politics/georgia-home-depot-boycott.html|access-date=April 20, 2021|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Georgia Governor [[Brian Kemp]] criticized the boycott, saying "this insanity needs to stop" and contending that it "puts partisan politics ahead of people's paychecks."<ref>{{cite web|last=Bowden|first=John|date=April 20, 2021|title=Georgia governor rips Home Depot boycott: 'This insanity needs to stop'|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/549291-georgia-governor-rips-home-depot-boycott-this-insanity-needs-to-stop|access-date=April 20, 2021|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|title=Foes of Ga. voter law boycott Home Depot; Kemp fires back|url=https://www.wrdw.com/2021/04/20/foes-of-ga-voter-law-to-launch-boycott-of-home-depot/|access-date=April 20, 2021|website=www.wrdw.com|date=April 20, 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

In 2023, Home Depot Vice President of Asset Protection Scott Glenn urged [[United States Congress|Congress]] to pass legislation aimed at combating organized retail crime groups by testifying before the [[United States House Committee on Homeland Security|House Homeland Security Committee's Subcommittee on Counterterrorism, Law Enforcement and Intelligence]]. The bill was introduced to Congress in early 2024 and would serve to increase federal coordination with state and local law enforcement in the fight against retail crime.<ref>{{Cite web|language=en|url=https://www.foxbusiness.com/lifestyle/home-depot-exec-calls-congress-pass-bipartisan-organized-retail-crime-bill|title=Home Depot exec calls on Congress to pass bipartisan organized retail crime bill|website=Fox Business|date=December 12, 2023 |access-date=2024-02-27|archive-date=2024-02-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240228005043/https://www.foxbusiness.com/lifestyle/home-depot-exec-calls-congress-pass-bipartisan-organized-retail-crime-bill}}</ref>

==Outside the United States==
===Canada===
[[File:Home Depot in Whitby, August 25 2025 (02).jpg|thumb|A Home Depot store in [[Whitby, Ontario]]]]
Home Depot Canada is the Canadian unit of the Home Depot and one of Canada's top home improvement retailers. The Canadian operation consists of 182 stores and employs over 28,000 people in Canada. Home Depot Canada has stores in all ten Canadian provinces and serves territorial Nunavut, Northwest Territories, and Yukon through electronic means (Online Sales). The Canadian head office is located in Toronto.

The Canadian unit was created with the purchase of [[Aikenhead's Hardware]]. Home Depot management had an ambitious plan to overtake its biggest competitor, [[Rona, Inc.|RONA]], which has about four times as many stores. However, some of RONA's stores are smaller than the typical Home Depot store. In terms of big box stores, the Home Depot has more stores than RONA (not including other Rona banners such as [[Réno-Dépôt]] or Cashway). As of 2007, RONA pulled ahead of The Home Depot in total retail sales, due to aggressive consolidation efforts by RONA, combined with the loss of The Home Depot's industrial supply division, HD Supply, in July 2007. The Home Depot faced competition from Lowe's after it entered the Canadian market at the end of 2007. In 2016, Lowe's purchased RONA, increasing its total store count to over 500 locations. In 2022, Lowe's announced it would sell its Canadian operations, including RONA, to [[Sycamore Partners]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-11-03 |title=Hardware giant Lowe's selling Canadian retail operations, including RONA, to private-equity firm |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-hardware-giant-lowes-selling-canadian-retail-operations-including-rona/ |access-date=2025-08-04 |work=The Globe and Mail |language=en-CA}}</ref>

[[File:The Home Depot logo (Quebec).svg|thumb|The Home Depot logo as used in Quebec.]]
In [[Quebec]], where it has 22 stores, The Home Depot is branded simply Home Depot (using English words but without the [[definite article]] "The"). The Canadian operation is a participant in the voluntary [[Scanner Price Accuracy Code]] managed by the [[Retail Council of Canada]].<ref name="Harris">{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/price-code-free-1.6263904|title=Attention shoppers: Overcharged for an item at checkout? You might be able to get it for free|last=Harris|first=Sophia|publisher=[[CBC News]]|date=28 November 2021|access-date=28 November 2021}}</ref>

===Mexico===
[[File:homedepot mxcentro.JPG|thumb|The Home Depot store in [[Mexico City|Mexico City, Mexico]].]]

The Home Depot operates 140 stores and employs more than 18,000 associates as of early 2025, making it one of the largest retailers in Mexico since entering the market in 2001. The company expanded its presence in 2004 with the acquisition of Home Mart, then the second-largest home improvement retailer in Mexico.<ref name="homedepot.com.mx">{{cite web |date=October 12, 2020 |title=Acerca de nosotros &#124; the Home Depot México |url=http://www.homedepot.com.mx/acerca-de-nosotros}}</ref>

In February 2025, The Home Depot announced it would invest $1.3 billion in Mexico over a three-year period, with plans to open five stores per year and generate 12,000 direct and indirect jobs.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rivera |first=Salvador |date=Feb 28, 2025 |title=Home Depot to invest $1.3 billion in Mexico |url=https://www.borderreport.com/news/trade/home-depot-to-invest-3-3-billion-in-mexico/ |work=Border Report}}</ref>

===China===
In December 2006, The Home Depot announced its acquisition of the Chinese home improvement retailer The Home Way. The acquisition gave The Home Depot an immediate presence in China, with 12 stores in six cities. In April 2011, Home Depot shut its last Beijing store, the fifth Home Depot to close in China in the previous two years. In September 2012, The Home Depot announced it was closing all big box stores in China. The Home Depot retained two specialty stores in China, a Home Decorators Collection Store and a paint and flooring store.<ref name="Burkitt">{{cite news|last=Burkitt|first=Laurie|title=Home Depot Learns Chinese Prefer 'Do-It-for-Me'|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10000872396390444433504577651072911154602|access-date=February 19, 2014|newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|date=September 14, 2012}}</ref>

As of September 16, 2012, all seven of the box stores in China had been shut down.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wantchinatimes.com/news-subclass-cnt.aspx?id=20120916000036&cid=1102|title=Home Depot closes China stores, denies 'moving out'|publisher=[[China Times]]|author=<!--Not stated-->|date=September 16, 2012|access-date=January 1, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029205903/http://www.wantchinatimes.com/news-subclass-cnt.aspx?id=20120916000036&cid=1102|archive-date=October 29, 2013}}</ref> The Home Depot has no immediate plans to further expand its specialty stores in China. The company is taking a "wait-and-see" attitude towards the Chinese market, but does not want to completely pull out because re-entry into the market would be very costly.

The Home Depot's lack of success in China has been attributed to the disconnect between The Home Depot's do-it-yourself ethos and Chinese culture. In 2012, The Home Depot conceded that it misread the country's appetite for do-it-yourself products. As a spokeswoman for the company said in an interview with the ''Wall Street Journal'', "The market trend says this is more of a do-it-for-me culture."<ref name="Burkitt"/> Some have speculated that The Home Depot could have offered a do-it-for-me model to Chinese consumers. Chinese consumers prefer to see a finished product, such as a renovated room, rather than light bulbs and lumber.<ref>{{cite web|last=Tulshyan|first=Ruchika|title=Home Depot's failure in China: Ignoring women|url=http://www.bizjournals.com/atlanta/blog/femme-fortune/2013/04/home-depots-failure-in-china.html?page=all|work=Atlanta Business Chronicle|access-date=February 19, 2014}}</ref> The same issue does not exist outside of China, especially in Canada, where Chinese Home Depot advertisements and store signage can be found in areas with large Chinese demographics.

===United Kingdom===
There were reports that The Home Depot was interested in acquiring [[B&Q]], the largest [[DIY]] retailer in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and China. B&Q had notably mimicked the design of Home Depot stores in the US when it introduced its large format "Warehouse" stores in the 1990s, even extending to changing its corporate colours to the same shade of orange as Home Depot. Speculation of a takeover began in 1999 when the retailer [[Asda]] was purchased by [[Walmart]]. The Home Depot would have to acquire [[Kingfisher plc]], B&Q's parent company, to acquire B&Q. Kingfisher consists of several European DIY chains; however, the Home Depot was only interested in B&Q operations and says that it would dispose of the [[Castorama]] chain which operates in France, Italy, Poland and Russia. Talks ending in 2005 did not result in any takeover deal.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/3368427.stm|work=[[BBC News]]|title=Bid Talk Lifts Kingfisher Shares|date= January 5, 2004|access-date=May 25, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://thescotsman.scotsman.com/business.cfm?id=497862005|title=The Scotsman|date=May 9, 2005|access-date=April 29, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051117134652/http://thescotsman.scotsman.com/business.cfm?id=497862005|archive-date=November 17, 2005}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.abcmoney.co.uk/news/2120062199.htm |title=Kingfisher profit down 33% as B&Q unit takes a hammering |date=March 21, 2006 |publisher=Abcmoney.co.uk |access-date=June 26, 2013 |archive-date=March 18, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120318054546/http://www.abcmoney.co.uk/news/2120062199.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===South America===
In 1993, Home Depot opened its first and only store in [[Peru]], however, low sales and weak promotion for the brand led to its closure the following year. In 1997, Home Depot entered the Chilean and Argentine markets. While the venture was viewed with great optimism by founders [[Bernard Marcus]] and [[Arthur Blank]],<ref name="Built from Scratch">{{Cite book|last1=Marcus|first1=Bernie|last2=Blank|first2=Arthur|last3=Andelman|first3=Bob|title=Built from Scratch|publisher=Random House|year=1999|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/builtfromscratch00marc_0/page/300 300–302]|isbn=0-8129-3058-4|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/builtfromscratch00marc_0/page/300}}</ref> it eventually proved unprofitable. In October 2001, Chilean partners [[Falabella (company)|Falabella]] bought out Home Depot's share of the five Chilean Home Center stores and rebranded them Home Store. In 2003, after merging with [[Sodimac]], all stores adopted that brand. The company has since expanded across Latin America very profitably and successfully. It's currently the largest home improvement company in South America.{{citation needed|date=June 2021}} In 2002, Argentina's Home Depots were bought out by Chilean company [[Cencosud]] and rebranded [[Easy (store)|Easy]] stores, a company that has also expanded across South America. It's the second largest home improvement company in South America.{{citation needed|date=June 2021}}

==Controversies==
===Whistleblower case===
{{More citations needed section|date=July 2022}}
The Home Depot was embroiled in [[whistleblower]] litigation brought under the [[Sarbanes-Oxley Act]] (SOX) law. In July 2005, former employee Michael Davis, represented by attorney [[Mark D. Schwartz]], filed a whistleblower lawsuit against the Home Depot, alleging that his discharge was in retaliation for refusing to make unwarranted back charges against vendors. Davis alleges that the Home Depot forced its employees to meet a set quota of back charges to cover damaged or defective merchandise, forcing employees to make chargebacks to vendors for merchandise that was undamaged and not defective. The Home Depot alleges that it fired Davis for repeatedly failing to show up for work.

The trial initially was concluded in June 2006, but in April 2007, U.S. Department of Labor Judge Pamela Lakes Wood ordered the case reopened after the Home Depot's law firm [[Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld]] revealed that the retail giant's in-house counsel had told them that two Home Depot employees who testified at the trial had lied. Akin Gump sent Wood a letter on September 29, 2006, in which the law firm requested that the testimony be stricken. In response to Akin Gump's revelation, Davis' attorney, Schwartz, asked for the case to be reopened to permit further questioning of the witnesses. On April 6, 2007, Wood ordered the case to be reopened.

The Home Depot settled the dispute. A stipulation of settlement dated March 28, 2008 was released. In the settlement, The Home Depot changed some of its corporate governance provisions. The Home Depot also agreed to pay the plaintiff's counsel $6 million in cash and $8.5 million in common stock.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/354950/000110465908023700/a08-10344_1ex99d2.htm |title=Home Depot Settlement |publisher=U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission |date=March 28, 2008}}</ref>

===Patent law controversy===
''[[Powell v. Home Depot USA, Inc.]]'' (2008cv61862) (2011) was a decision by the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida]] concerning [[patent infringement]] on a "safe hands" device that Michael Powell, an independent contractor for Home Depot, created in response to injuries to the hands of associates using in-store radial arm saws. The district court jury returned a verdict in favor of Powell.

In 2011, Home Depot appealed against the decision to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit]], challenging the district court's denial of its renewed motion for judgment as a matter of law on the issues of infringement, willfulness, and damages.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.patents4life.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/11/10-1409-1416.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021054507/http://www.patents4life.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/11/10-1409-1416.pdf|url-status=live|title=United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit|archive-date=October 21, 2012|publisher=Patent4Life|author=Michael S. Powell}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Powell v. Home Depot – False Petition Not "Egregious Misconduct"|url=http://www.natlawreview.com/article/powell-v-home-depot-false-petition-not-egregious-misconduct|publisher=Schwegman, Lundberg & Woessner, P.A.|work=The [[National Law Review]]|date=November 16, 2011|access-date=September 13, 2012}}</ref> They also challenged the district court's claim construction, [[inequitable conduct]], and attorney fees determinations. The appellate court found no inequitable conduct and insufficiently egregious misconduct on the part of Powell's attorney.<ref>{{cite web |title=Post-Therasense: Inequitable Conduct Really Is a Higher Standard|url=http://www.natlawreview.com/article/post-therasense-inequitable-conduct-really-higher-standard|publisher=[[McDermott Will & Emery]]|date=December 5, 2011|access-date=September 3, 2012}}</ref>

===Tilt-up construction design of stores===
[[File:The appliances section of a Home Depot store in Blairsville, Ga.jpg|thumb|The appliances section inside a Home Depot store]]
In the wake of the [[2011 Joplin tornado]] in which the walls of a Home Depot collapsed after being hit by an [[EF5 tornado]], ''[[The Kansas City Star]]'', citing engineers, criticized Home Depot's practice of using [[tilt-up]] construction in hundreds of its big-box stores (other nearby big-box stores in Joplin, including a [[Walmart]] and [[Academy Sports + Outdoors]], which had [[Concrete masonry unit|concrete block]] construction, lost their roofs but the walls remained intact). In tilt-up construction, the concrete is poured onsite, lifted into place, and then attached to the roof. The engineers told the ''Star'' that the practice, while normally safe and efficient, is dangerous in major storms because once the roof is lifted (as happened in Joplin) the walls collapse in a [[domino effect]]. Seven people were killed in the front of the store when the 100,000-pound walls collapsed on them, while 28 people in the back of the store survived when those walls collapsed outward. Only two of the slab walls in the Home Depot survived. In contrast, three people died in the Walmart but 200 survived. Engineers noted that when concrete block construction fails, structural elements break in pieces and usually not in huge slabs. Home Depot said it fundamentally disagreed with the engineers quoted by the ''Star'' and said it would use tilt-up construction in the rebuilt Joplin store.<ref>{{cite web| author = McGraw, Mike |date=June 25, 2011|url=http://www.kansascity.com/2011/06/25/2975177/experts-challenge-building-design.html#ixzz1QZoEgC5d|title=Experts Challenge Home Depot Building Design, Codes After Joplin Tornado|work=[[The Kansas City Star]]|access-date=June 28, 2011}}</ref>

===Payment-system breach===
{{anchor|Home Depot data breach}}
{{See also|List of data breaches in the United States}}
[[File:HomeDepotPinOakHoustonselfcheckout.jpg|thumb|upright|Self-checkout system]]

On September 2, 2014, security news reporter [[Brian Krebs]] reported that he was seeing evidence of credit card numbers linked to Home Depot purchases being sold online, which he concluded to suggest that The Home Depot's payment systems were breached by hackers.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://krebsonsecurity.com/2014/09/banks-credit-card-breach-at-home-depot/|title=Banks: Credit Card Breach at Home Depot |publisher=[[Krebs on Security]] |date=September 2, 2014 }}</ref> On September 8, 2014, Home Depot confirmed that its payment systems were compromised.<ref>{{cite web|title=Customer Update on Payment Breach|publisher=The Home Depot|website=Corporate.HomeDepot.com|url=https://corporate.homedepot.com/MediaCenter/Pages/Statement1.aspx|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140914000750/https://corporate.homedepot.com/MediaCenter/Pages/Statement1.aspx|archive-date=September 14, 2014|access-date=September 14, 2019}}</ref> According to its press release, this breach affected any customers who made purchases at any Home Depot store from April 2014 to September 2014. Home Depot offered its affected customers a free one-year credit monitoring service from [[AllClear ID]]. Also in its press release, it made sure to emphasize that there was no evidence to suggest that online customers were affected by the breach. On September 18, 2014, Home Depot released a statement saying that the hackers obtained a total of [http://krebsonsecurity.com/2014/09/home-depot-56m-cards-impacted-malware-contained/ 56 million credit card numbers] as a result of the breach. Since the breach, Home Depot has rolled out new encryption technology for its cash registers and self-checkout systems to protect customers. A class-action lawsuit was filed against the company.

In March 2016, Home Depot agreed to pay at least $19.5 million to compensate the more than 50 million consumers affected. The settlement terms included a $13 million fund to reimburse shoppers and a $6.5 million fund for cardholder identity protection services.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-home-depot-breach-settlement-idUSKCN0WA24Z|title=Home Depot Settles Consumer Lawsuit over Big 2014 Data Breach |work=[[Reuters]] |date=March 8, 2016 }}</ref>

===EEOC disability discrimination suit===
In September 2012, Home Depot agreed to pay $100,000 and furnish other relief to settle a [[disability]] discrimination lawsuit<ref>{{cite web|title=Complaint, U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Home Depot USA Inc.|url=https://www.pacermonitor.com/view/PMOABZY/US_Equal_Employment_Opportunity_v_Home_Depot_USA_Inc__mddce-12-01952__0001.0.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160809103919/https://www.pacermonitor.com/view/PMOABZY/US_Equal_Employment_Opportunity_v_Home_Depot_USA_Inc__mddce-12-01952__0001.0.pdf|archive-date=August 9, 2016|website=PacerMonitor|access-date=June 16, 2016}}</ref> filed by the U.S. [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission]], for the alleged failure to provide a [[reasonable accommodation]] for a cashier with cancer at its [[Towson, Maryland]], store and then for purportedly firing her because of her condition.<ref>{{cite web|title=Home Depot to Pay $100,000 to Settle EEOC Disability Discrimination Suit
|url=http://www.natlawreview.com/article/home-depot-to-pay-100000-to-settle-eeoc-disability-discrimination-suit |publisher=U.S. [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission]] |work=The National Law Review|date=September 10, 2012|access-date=September 23, 2012}}</ref>

===Lead paint===
In December 2020, The Home Depot was fined $20.75 million for [[lead paint]] violations.<ref name=JusticeLead>{{cite web |url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/home-depot-pay-20750000-penalty-nationwide-failure-follow-rules-conducting-renovations |title=Home Depot to Pay $20,750,000 Penalty for Nationwide Failure to Follow Rules for Conducting Renovations Involving Lead Paint |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=December 17, 2020 |website=Justice News |publisher=[[US Department of Justice]] |access-date=March 20, 2021 |quote=Home Depot will also pay a $20.75 million penalty, the highest civil penalty obtained to date for a settlement under the Toxic Substances Control Act.}}</ref><ref name=EpaLead>{{cite web |url=https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/home-depot-settlement-information-sheet |title=Home Depot Settlement Information Sheet |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=December 17, 2020 |website=Environmental Topics/Enforcement |publisher=[[US Environmental Protection Agency]] |access-date=March 20, 2021 |quote=Home Depot frequently subcontracted work to uncertified firms, did not use lead-safe work practices, did not perform required post-renovation cleaning, did not provide the EPA-required lead-based paint pamphlets to occupants, and did not establish records of compliance}}</ref> Home Depot were accused of hiring contractors for its home renovation services who did not use proper lead abatement procedures during renovation projects.<ref name=EpaLead/><ref name=JusticeLead/>

=== ICE crackdown ===
{{Immigration policy of the second Trump administration sidebar| expanded=technology}}

==== Targeting of undocumented workers ====

Home Depot has had a decades-long track record as a gathering place for workers who are undocumented immigrants, many who work as roofers, painters, or construction workers.<ref>{{cite news |last=Greenhouse |first=Steven |date=10 October 2005 |title=Day Laborer Battle Runs Outside Home Depot |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/10/10/us/day-laborer-battle-runs-outside-home-depot.html |newspaper=The New York Times |url-access=subscription |access-date=23 January 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=cnnice />

In May 2025, top White House official [[Stephen Miller]] directed ICE to target Home Depot day laborers to find undocumented immigrants to deport.<ref name=wsjice>{{cite news |last1=Findell |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Simon |first2=Ruth |last3=Hackman |first3=Michelle |last4=Parti |first4=Tarini |date=9 June 2025 |title=The White House Marching Orders That Sparked the L.A. Migrant Crackdown |url=https://www.wsj.com/us-news/protests-los-angeles-immigrants-trump-f5089877 |work=The Wall Street Journal |access-date=23 January 2026 |language=en}}</ref> The [[Washington Post]] reported that "ICE agents appeared to follow Miller's tip and conducted an immigration sweep Friday at the Home Depot in the predominantly Latino neighborhood of [[Westlake, Los Angeles|Westlake]] in [[Los Angeles]]."<ref name=wsjice /> One man going to a Home Depot in Westlake noticed the men who regularly gather outside looking for work were missing.<ref name=npr /> Earlier that day, a moving van containing a group of federal agents wearing border patrol vests pulled up to a Home Depot, at which point the back door opened and the agents "ran into the parking lot" and detained 16 people.<ref>{{cite web |last=Rainey |first=Libby |date=6 August 2025 |title=Federal agents detain people at a Westlake Home Depot after jumping out of rented Penske moving van |url=https://laist.com/news/federal-agents-westlake-home-depot-penske-moving-van |website=LAist |publisher=Southern California Public Radio |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251102211459/https://laist.com/news/federal-agents-westlake-home-depot-penske-moving-van |archive-date=November 2, 2025 |url-status=bot: unknown |access-date=23 January 2026 |language=en }}</ref> One undocumented day laborer told [[CNN]], "Right now, I'm behind on my rent because I'm scared of getting detained at the corner of Home Depot or having an encounter with ICE."<ref name=cnnice>{{cite news |last=Meyersohn |first=Nathaniel |date=18 July 2025 |title=How Home Depot became a magnet for day laborers and a target for ICE |url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/07/18/business/home-depot-ice-day-laborers |work=CNN |access-date=23 January 2026 |language=en}}</ref> On [[Reddit]], some Home Depot workers shared stories about how raids had caused fewer contractors to visit stores, whereas others said nothing had changed.<ref name=npr />

In a social media post, Home Depot downplayed the incidents, claiming that employees were told to report incidents and avoid interactions with immigration agents,<ref name=cnnice /><ref name=npr /> and referring to a mandate to follow "all federal and local rules and regulations."<ref name=njm /><ref name=npr /> NPR characterized Home Depot as "keeping quiet" in the midst of immigration raids at their stores across the country.<ref name=npr>{{cite news |last1=Selyukh |first1=Alina |last2=Baker |first2=Liz |date=19 August 2025 |title=Home Depot keeps quiet on immigration raids outside its doors |url=https://www.npr.org/2025/08/19/nx-s1-5504124/home-depot-earnings-immigration-raids-day-laborers |work=NPR |publisher=National Public Radio |access-date=23 January 2026 |language=en}}</ref> ICE raids have not significantly impacted Home Depot sales.<ref name=npr />

==== Protests ====
[[File:New York City January 23 2026 anti-ICE protest stops outside Home Depot.webm|thumb|upright=0.65|Anti-ICE protest outside Home Depot, [[New York City]], January 2026]]

After the ICE raids at Home Depot, Home Depot has been the target of anti-[[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement|ICE]] protests at stores in [[Mercer County, New Jersey]], [[Los Angeles]], [[Ladera Heights]], [[Greenfield, Indiana]], and [[New York City]].<ref name=njm /><ref name=tipranks>{{cite web |last=Anderson |first=Steve |date=22 January 2026 |title=Anti-ICE Protests Shut Home Depot Store: Home Depot Stock (NYSE:HD) Slips |url=https://www.tipranks.com/news/anti-ice-protests-shut-home-depot-store-home-depot-stock-nysehd-slips |website=TipRanks |access-date=23 January 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Hoffman |first=Erin-Leigh |date=20 January 2026 |title=Local activists demand The Home Depot condemn ICE raids |url=https://recorder.com/2026/01/20/greenfield-home-depot-ice-protest/ |website=Greenfield Recorder |access-date=23 January 2026 |language=en}}</ref> In Mercer County, one protester said "We want Home Depot to do something, to pass a policy, to say something."<ref name=njm>{{cite web |last=Nieto-Munoz |first=Sophie |date=19 December 2025 |title=Anti-ICE protestors target Home Depot to denounce immigration arrests |url=https://newjerseymonitor.com/briefs/anti-ice-protestors-target-home-depot-to-denounce-immigration-arrests/ |website=New Jersey Monitor |publisher=States Newsroom |access-date=23 January 2026 |language=en}}</ref> 50 protesters with ICE Out of New Jersey bought $2.97 ice scrapers in New Jersey and immediately returned it to stall the store's operations,<ref name=njm /> a type of protest used at other Home Depot stores across the country.<ref name=tipranks /> Protesters also urged shoppers to boycott Home Depot.<ref name=njm /> Police arrived and told protesters to leave the property.<ref name=njm /> In Ladera Heights, during an ice scraper protest focused on Home Depot's "complicity" in "violating civil rights," a store was shut down for the day in its entirety.<ref name=tipranks /> One activist said "I think they have a responsibility and certainly a moral obligation to defend day laborers."<ref name=npr />

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Home improvement
======================================================================

{{Short description|Process of renovating or making additions to one's home}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=June 2013}}
{{About||the 1990s sitcom|Home Improvement (TV series)|other uses}}
{{Multiple issues|
{{more citations needed|date=June 2008}}
{{prose|date=January 2017}}
}}
[[File:Front doors in a home improvement store in the US 2.jpg|thumb|right|Merchandise on display in a hardware store]]
'''Home improvement''' is the process of [[renovation|renovating]], improving or adding to one's home.<ref>{{cite web | title=Home improvement | url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/us/dictionary/english/home-improvement }}</ref> Home improvement can consist of [[project]]s that upgrade an existing home interior (such as electrical and plumbing), exterior (masonry, concrete, siding, roofing) or other improvements to the property (i.e. garden work or garage maintenance/additions). Home improvement projects can be carried out for a number of different reasons: personal preference and comfort, maintenance or repair work, making a home bigger by adding rooms/spaces, as a means of saving energy, or to improve safety.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/us/dictionary/english/home-improvements|title=HOME IMPROVEMENTS definition in American English &#124; Collins English Dictionary|date=February 13, 2020|website=www.collinsdictionary.com}}</ref>

==Types of home improvement==

While "home improvement" often refers to building projects that alter the structure of an existing home, it can also include improvements to lawns, gardens, and outdoor structures, such as gazebos and garages. It also encompasses maintenance, repair, and general servicing tasks. Home improvement projects generally have one or more of the following goals:{{citation needed|date=October 2019}}

===Comfort===
*Upgrading [[heating]], [[Ventilation (architecture)|ventilation]] and [[air conditioning]] systems ([[HVAC]]).
*Upgrading rooms with luxuries, such as adding [[gourmet]] features to a kitchen or a [[hot tub]] [[spa]] to a bathroom.
*Increasing the capacity of [[plumbing]] and [[electrical]] systems.
*[[Waterproofing]] [[basement]]s.
*[[Soundproofing]] rooms, especially bedrooms and baths.

===Maintenance and repair===
[[File:Home improvement (4777036919).jpg|thumb|right|Man painting a fence]]
Maintenance projects can include:
*[[Roof]] tear-off and replacement.
*Replacement or new construction windows.
*[[Concrete]] and [[masonry]] repairs to the [[foundation (architecture)|foundation]] and [[chimney]].
*Repainting rooms, walls or [[fence]]s
*Repairing [[plumbing]] and [[electrical]] systems
*[[Wallpaper|Wallpapering]] 
*[[Wood finishing|Furniture polishing]]
*Plumbing, home interior and exterior works
*Shower maintenance

===Additional space===
Additional living space may be added by:
*Turning marginal areas into livable spaces such as turning basements into [[recreation room|recrooms]], [[home cinema|home theater]]s, or [[small office/home office|home office]]s – or [[attic]]s into spare [[bedroom]]s.
*Extending one's house with rooms added to the side of one's home or, sometimes, extra levels to the original [[roof]]. Such a new unit of construction is called an "add-on".<ref>{{cite web|title=Add-on|url=https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/us/add-on|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170221105404/https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/us/add-on|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 21, 2017|website=English Oxford Living Dictionary (US)|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|access-date=20 February 2017}}</ref>

===Saving energy===
Homeowners may reduce [[public utility|utility]] costs with:
*[[Efficient energy use|Energy-efficient]] [[thermal insulation]], [[replacement window]]s, and [[lighting]].
*[[Renewable energy]] with [[biomass]] [[pellet stove]]s, wood-burning [[stove]]s, [[Photovoltaic module|solar panel]]s, [[wind turbine]]s, [[programmable thermostat]]s,<ref>[http://www.oldhouseweb.com/green-guide/use-a-programmable-thermostat-common-sense-to-reduce-energy-bills.shtml Use a Programmable Thermostat, Common Sense, to Reduce Energy Bills] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090719094643/http://www.oldhouseweb.com/green-guide/use-a-programmable-thermostat-common-sense-to-reduce-energy-bills.shtml |date=July 19, 2009 }}, Brett Freeman, oldhouseweb.com</ref> and [[geothermal exchange heat pump]]s (see [[autonomous building]]).

=== Safety, emergency management, security and privacy ===
The need to be safer or for better [[privacy]] or [[emergency management]] can be fulfilled with diversified measures which can be improved, maintained or added. [[Hidden compartment|Secret compartments]] and [[secret passage|passages]] can also be conceived for [[privacy]] and [[security]].

* Interventions for [[fire protection]] and avoidance. Possible examples are [[fire sprinkler system]]s for [[automatic fire suppression]], [[smoke detectors]] for [[fire detection]], [[fire alarm systems]], or [[passive fire protection]] (including some [[wildfire#Prevention|wildfire management]] strategies).
* Technical solutions to increase protection from [[natural disasters]], or [[geotechnical engineering|geotechnical]] and [[Structural integrity and failure|structural safety]] (e.g. [[tropical_cyclone_preparedness#Home_retrofitting|hurricane]] or [[seismic retrofit]]).
* Interventions and additions to increase [[home safety]] from other hazards, like [[Falling (accident)|falls]], [[electric injury|electric injuries]], [[gas leaks]] or home exposure to [[Environmental health#Concerns|environmental health concerns]].
* [[Physical security]] measures:
** [[Access control]] systems and physical barriers, which can include [[Fence|fences]], physical [[door security|door]] and [[window security]] measures (e.g. [[grille (architecture)|grilles]], [[laminated glass]], [[window shutters]]), [[Lock and key|locks]];
** [[Security lighting]], [[security alarms]] and [[video surveillance]].
* [[Safes]] and [[bank vault|vaults]].
* Spaces for [[emergency evacuation]], like [[Emergency exit|emergency exits]] and rarer [[escape tunnel|escape tunnels]].
* Spaces which provide protection in the event of different [[emergencies]]: [[area of refuge|areas of refuge]], [[storm cellar|storm cellars]] (as protection from [[tornadoes]] and other kinds of [[severe weather]]), [[panic room|panic rooms]], [[bunkers]] and [[bomb shelter|bomb shelters]] (including [[fallout shelters]]), etc.
* Home renovations or additions used to increase [[privacy]] can be as simple as [[curtains]] or much more advanced, such as some [[Countersurveillance#Structural countermeasures|structural surveillance counter-measures]]. They may overlap with [[physical security]] measures.
* [[Public utility]] outage preparedness, like [[Standby generator|backup generators]] for providing power during [[power outage]]s .

==Home improvement industry==
[[File:010 Screws and bolts in OBI home improvement store in Poland.jpg|thumb|right|Screws and bolts in an [[OBI (retail chain)|OBI]] home improvement store in [[Poland]]]]
{{Further|Hardware store}}
Home or [[residential]] renovation is an almost $300 billion industry in the United States,<ref name="JCHS">{{Cite web |url=http://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/jchs.harvard.edu/files/r07-1.pdf |title=Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University, 2007 |access-date=April 10, 2014 |archive-date=August 7, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140807204656/http://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/jchs.harvard.edu/files/r07-1.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> and a $48 billion industry in Canada.<ref name="CMHC">{{cite web|url=http://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/|title=Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation - Société canadienne d'hypothèques et de logement|access-date=October 23, 2007|archive-date=October 23, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071023072751/http://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/|url-status=live}}</ref>{{full citation needed|date=June 2012}} The average cost per project is $3,000 in the United States and $11,000–15,000 in Canada.

Professional home improvement is ancient and goes back to the beginning of recorded civilization. One example is [[Sergius Orata]], who in the 1st century B.C. is said by the writer [[Vitruvius]] (in his famous book [[De architectura]]) to have invented the [[hypocaust]]. The hypocaust is an underfloor heating system that was used throughout the [[Roman Empire]] in villas of the wealthy. He is said to have become wealthy himself by buying villas at a low price, adding [[spa]]s and his newly invented hypocaust, and reselling them at higher prices.<ref name="CHTT">{{cite web|url=https://homeownersgta.online/home-renovation-guides/5-low-cost-advices-for-home-improvement-that-boost-the-sale-of-your-home|title=Canada Homeowners Community - Example of Low-Cost Advices used by Canadian Homeowners (Community) for Home Improvement that boost the sale of your Home|date=January 12, 2020 |publisher=Canada Homeowners Community}}</ref>

===Renovation contractors===
Perhaps the most important or visible professionals in the renovation industry are renovation contractors or skilled trades. These are the [[general contractor|builders]] that have specialized [[credentials]], licensing and experience to perform renovation services in specific [[municipalities]].

While there is a fairly large "grey market" of unlicensed companies, there are those that have membership in a reputable association and/or are accredited by a professional organization. Homeowners are recommended to perform checks such as verifying license and insurance and checking business references prior to hiring a contractor to work on their house.

Lifestyle publications often provide guidance for homeowners on budget-conscious upgrades, emphasizing strategies to refresh living spaces quickly and affordably.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kalinowski |first=Allison |title=Tips To Make Your Home Feel Like New This Weekend |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/tips-make-home-feel-like-new-weekend_l_5e8cad71c5b6e1d10a6aacc6 |work=HuffPost |date=April 7, 2020 |access-date=September 22, 2025}}</ref>

Because interior renovation will touch the change of the internal structure of the house, ceiling construction, circuit configuration and partition walls, etc., such work related to the structure of the house, of course, also includes renovation of wallpaper posting, furniture settings, lighting, etc.

===Aggregators===
Aggregators are companies that bundle home improvement service offers and act as intermediary agency between service providers and customers.

==In popular culture==
Home improvement was popularized on television in 1979 with the premiere of ''[[This Old House]]'' starring [[Bob Vila]] on PBS. American cable channel [[HGTV]] features many do-it-yourself shows, as does sister channel [[DIY Network]].<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Cerone|first1=Daniel|title=Tim Allen's Power Tools : Television: The comic who had Disney and cable executives abuzz parlayed his luck to develop 'Home Improvement|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1991-09-17-ca-2925-story.html|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=17 September 1991|access-date=16 June 2015|archive-date=June 22, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150622023606/http://articles.latimes.com/1991-09-17/entertainment/ca-2925_1_tim-allen|url-status=live}}</ref>
[[Danny Lipford]] hosts and produces the nationally syndicated ''[[Today's Homeowner with Danny Lipford]]''. [[Tom Kraeutler]] and [[Leslie Segrete]] co-host the nationally syndicated ''[[The Money Pit Home Improvement Radio Show]]''.

Movies that poked fun at the difficulties involved include: ''[[Mr. Blandings Builds His Dream House]]'' (1948), starring [[Cary Grant]] and [[Myrna Loy]]; ''[[George Washington Slept Here]]'' (1942), featuring [[Jack Benny]] and [[Ann Sheridan]]; and ''[[The Money Pit]]'' (1986), with [[Tom Hanks]] and [[Shelley Long]]. The sitcom ''[[Home Improvement (TV series)|Home Improvement]]'' used the home improvement [[Theme (literature)|theme]] for comedic purposes.
