The '''hospitality industry''' is a broad [[industry (economics)|category of fields]] within the [[service industry]] that includes [[lodging]], [[Food service|food and beverage services]], [[event planning]], [[Amusement park|theme parks]], [[water parks]], [[travel agency]], [[tourism]], [[hotel]]s, [[casino]]s, [[real estate]], [[restaurant]]s, [[nightclub]]s, and [[Bar (establishment)|bars]].

==Sectors==
According to the Cambridge Business English Dictionary the "hospitality industry" consists of hotels and food service,<ref>{{cite web |title=Hospitality industry |url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/us/dictionary/english/hospitality-industry |website=Cambridge Business English Dictionary |access-date=19 March 2020}}</ref> equivalent to [[NAICS]] code 72, "Accommodation and Food Service".

===Definition in the United States===
In 2020, the [[United States Department of Labor]] [[Standard Industrial Classification]] (SIC) defines the hospitality industry more broadly, including:<ref>{{cite web |title=Global Hospitality Leadership: Industry & Company Information |url=https://guides.library.georgetown.edu/c.php?g=76036&p=487475 |website=Georgetown University Library |access-date=19 March 2020}}</ref>
* 701 Hotels and Motels, including auto courts, [[bed and breakfast]] inns, cabins and cottages, [[casino]] hotels, [[hostel]]s, [[Hotel|hotels]] (except residential ones), [[inn]]s furnishing food and lodging, [[motel]]s, recreational hotels, [[Resort hotel|resort hotels]], seasonal hotels, [[ski lodge]]s and [[Resort|resorts]], tourist cabins and tourist courts

* 704 Organization Hotels and Lodging Houses, On a Membership Basis
* 58 Eating and Drinking Places (cf. U.S. "[[food service|food service industry]]", U.K. "[[foodservice|catering industry]]")
** 5812 Eating Places, including [[restaurants]] (among which carry-out restaurants, [[drive-in restaurant]]s and [[fast food]] restaurants), [[automat]]s, beaneries, box lunch stands, [[buffet]]s, [[café]]s, [[cafeteria]]s, [[caterer]]s, [[Diner|coffee shops]], commissary restaurants a.k.a. [[Cafeteria|canteens]], [[concession stand]]s, [[dhaba]] , [[Military hotels in Bengaluru|military hotel]] prepared food (e.g., in airports and sports arenas), contract feeding, dairy bars, diners, dining rooms, [[dinner theater]]s, food bars, [[frozen custard]] stands, grills, hamburger stands, [[hot dog stands]], ice cream stands, industrial feeding, institutional food service such as that aboard airplanes, railroads, and ships), lunch bars, [[lunch counter]]s, [[luncheonette]]s, [[lunchroom]]s, [[oyster bar]]s, [[pizza parlor]]s and [[pizzeria]]s, refreshment stands, sandwich bars or shops, snack shops, [[soda fountain]]s, soft drink stands, [[submarine sandwich]] shops, and [[tearooms]]. Sources other than the SIC also mention other formats of eating places such as [[cyber café]]s, [[ramen shop]]s a.k.a. noodle bars, and [[Conveyor belt sushi|sushi bars]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Andrews |title=Introduction To Tourism And Hospitality Industry |date=2007 |publisher=McGraw-Hill Education (India) |isbn=9780070660212 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PrRdc5SI_R4C |access-date=19 March 2020}}</ref>
** 5813 Drinking Places (alcoholic beverages) including [[Bar (establishment)|bar]]s, [[beer garden]]s/parlors/taverns, sale of beer, wine, and liquors for on-premise consumption, [[bottle club]]s, cabarets, [[cocktail lounge]]s, [[discotheque]]s, drinking places, [[nightclub]]s, [[Bar (establishment)|saloons]], [[taproom]]s, [[tavern]]s, and [[wine bars]]
* 472 Arrangement of Passenger Transportation
** 4724 [[travel agency|Travel Agencies]]
** 4725 [[tour operator|Tour Operators]]
** 4729 Arrangement of Passenger Transportation, Not Elsewhere Classified, such as [[Train ticket|ticket office]]s not operated by transportation companies, and services that arrange [[carpool]]s

In the United States, hotels are the most popular vacation accommodation. In 2022, the hotel and motel industry in the United States was a $224.9 billion market, measured by revenue.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hotels & Motels in the US - Market Size 2005–2029 |url=https://www.ibisworld.com/industry-statistics/market-size/hotels-motels-united-states/ |website=IBISWorld |access-date=6 August 2023}}</ref>

===Definition in Dutch, Italian and French===
'''Horeca''' (also '''HoReCa''', '''HORECA''') is the [[Dutch language|Dutch]], [[Indonesian language|Indonesian]], [[German language|German]], [[Italian language|Italian]], [[Romanian language|Romanian]], [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]] and [[French language|French]] term for the food service and hotel industries. The term is a [[syllabic abbreviation]] of the words [[hotel]]/[[restaurant]]/[[café]].<ref name="Eurostat">{{cite web|title=Abbreviations and Acronyms|url=http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/ramon/cybernews/abbreviations.htm#H|publisher=Eurostat|access-date=28 February 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Wat valt onder horeca? ("What is included in 'horeca'?") |url=https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/faq/specifiek/wat-valt-onder-horeca- |website=CBS (Central Bureau for Statistics of The Netherlands) |access-date=19 March 2020 |language=nl}}</ref> The term is mostly used in the [[Benelux]] countries, [[Indonesia]], and [[Switzerland]].

"Horeca" is often not a one-to-one equivalent to the term "hospitality industry" used in English, which is often used more broadly. According to the Cambridge Business English Dictionary the "hospitality industry" consists of hotels and food service,<ref>{{cite web |title=Hospitality industry |url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/us/dictionary/english/hospitality-industry |website=Cambridge Business English Dictionary |access-date=19 March 2020}}</ref> equivalent to [[NAICS]] code 72, "Accommodation and Food Service". However, the [[United States Department of Labor]] Standard Industry Classification (SIC) defines the hospitality industry more broadly, as noted above.

The Dutch ''Uniforme Voorwaarden Horeca'' (UVH) is translated into English as Uniform Conditions for the Hotel and Catering Industry. This code covers hotels, bars, restaurants and related businesses in the Netherlands. ''Koninklijke Horeca Nederland'' is the Dutch trade association for the hotel and catering industry.<ref>[http://www.horeca.org/smartsite.dws?id=3247 Uniform Conditions for the Hotel and Catering Industry – Koninklijk Horeca Nederland<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

This sector is one of the fastest growing in Europe. In 2004, more than 7.8 million people were employed<ref>[[Eurostat]], 2005</ref> and the sector generated more than $338 billion in turnover.<ref>[https://quantrinhahang.edu.vn/hoc-quan-ly-khach-san Hospitality industry course<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> Jobs tend to be temporary, with irregular hours, low pay, and few career prospects. There is a high proportion of young people working in the sector. Some distribution companies use this term to define the food & beverage service trade channel or the hospitality trade.

==Impact of the COVID‑19 Pandemic==
The COVID‑19 pandemic profoundly disrupted the hospitality industry, exposing its vulnerability to global crises. Hotels, restaurants, bars, and travel services experienced abrupt closures, reduced occupancy, and strict hygiene regulations, resulting in significant revenue losses and temporary layoffs. Research on adaptive legal literacy during the pandemic highlights that managers who successfully navigated this period relied on the ability to quickly interpret and apply shifting public health directives, labor laws, and safety regulations. This competency enabled hospitality professionals to implement effective hygiene protocols, manage workforce challenges, and maintain customer trust while complying with evolving governmental mandates. The experience underscored the importance of legal awareness, crisis management, and operational adaptability in sustaining resilience across lodging, food and beverage services, and other hospitality sectors.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Green |first1=Daniel |last2=Varburgh |first2=Januš C. |title=Adaptive Legal Literacy in Crisis: Responsible Hotel Management During the COVID‑19 Pandemic |journal=International Journal for the Semiotics of Law – Revue internationale de Sémiotique juridique |volume=39 |pages=1033–1077 |year=2026 |doi=10.1007/s11196-025-10395-5 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11196-025-10395-5
 |access-date=20 February 2026 |type=journal|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Technology ==

Hospitality operations rely on several categories of specialized software. The [[property management system]] (PMS) serves as the central operational platform for lodging properties, handling reservations, room assignment, guest check-in and check-out, housekeeping status, and guest billing.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kasavana |first1=Michael L. |last2=Brooks |first2=Richard M. |title=Managing Front Office Operations |edition=9th |publisher=American Hotel & Lodging Educational Institute |year=2013 |isbn=9780866123549}}</ref> Historically installed on premises, PMS platforms have increasingly migrated to cloud-based delivery, reducing on-property information technology infrastructure and enabling centralized management across multi-property portfolios.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Ivanov |first=Stanislav |title=Adoption of robots, artificial intelligence and service automation by travel, tourism and hospitality companies |journal=Zeitschrift für Tourismuswissenschaft |year=2019 |volume=11 |issue=1}}</ref>

[[Revenue management]] systems apply demand forecasting and pricing algorithms to set room rates dynamically. The discipline originated in the airline industry following deregulation in the United States and was subsequently adopted by hotel chains beginning in the 1980s.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Kimes |first=Sheryl E. |title=The Basics of Yield Management |journal=Cornell Hotel and Restaurant Administration Quarterly |year=1989 |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=14–19 |doi=10.1177/001088048903000309|hdl=1813/71953 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Distribution technology connects properties to booking channels. A central reservation system manages rate and inventory data, while a channel manager distributes that data to [[online travel agency|online travel agencies]], [[global distribution system|global distribution systems]], and a property's own booking engine.<ref>{{cite book |last=Ivanov |first=Stanislav |title=Hotel Revenue Management: From Theory to Practice |publisher=Zangador |year=2014 |isbn=9789549278118}}</ref>

Additional operational systems include [[point of sale]] platforms for food and beverage outlets, labor management and scheduling software, and [[business intelligence]] tools that consolidate data across these systems for performance reporting.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kasavana |first1=Michael L. |last2=Brooks |first2=Richard M. |title=Managing Front Office Operations |edition=9th |publisher=American Hotel & Lodging Educational Institute |year=2013 |isbn=9780866123549}}</ref>

== By country ==
=== India ===
The hotel industry in [[India]] is poised for continued strong growth, with [[CareEdge Group|CareEdge Ratings]] forecasting a 9-11% year-over-year increase in revenue for hotels in FY25. This comes after an estimated 12-14% growth in [[RevPAR]] (revenue per available room) in FY24, driven by robust demand outpacing supply.<ref>{{cite news |last1=V |first1=Manju |title=Hotels to see 9-11% Revenue Growth in FY25: CareEdge Ratings. |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/hotels-to-see-9-11-revenue-growth-in-fy25-careedge-ratings-report/articleshow/108850321.cms |access-date=17 June 2024 |publisher=The Times of India |date=28 March 2024}}</ref> Average room rates across India are projected to rise from around ₹7,200-7,400 in FY24 to ₹7,700-7,900 in FY25, with RevPAR climbing to an average of ₹4,800-5,000 by end-FY24. The recovery is fueled by healthy domestic leisure and business travel demand, complemented by increasing foreign tourist arrivals. While new supply is expected at a 4-5% CAGR over 4-5 years adding over 50,000 branded rooms, this delayed catch-up will allow demand-supply dynamics to gradually align. The CareEdge report notes a better balance emerging across segments like upscale, upper midscale and midscale/economy, reducing the earlier concentration in luxury/upper upscale. With high occupancies of 68-70% forecast for FY25, the strong RevPAR growth should aid in improving the credit profile of industry players.

=== United Kingdom ===
{{main|Hospitality industry in the United Kingdom}}
In 2015 the [[United Kingdom]] hospitality industry employed around 2.9m people – around 9% of the UK workforce.<ref>{{Cite web |title=International Marketing Mix of ITC Hotels in UK {{!}} PDF {{!}} Economies {{!}} Marketing |url=https://www.scribd.com/document/540866107/International-Marketing-Mix-of-ITC-hotels-in-UK |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=Scribd |language=en}}</ref> By employment, it is the UK's fourth-largest industry. The most jobs in the industry are found in London (around 500,000) and [[South East England]] (around 400,000); 18% of workers in the UK industry are in London. There are around 1.5m restaurant workers, and around 0.5m work in hotels. The [[Food Safety Act 1990]] introduced the training that staff have to follow. Around 25% of the hospitality workforce comes from the EU, making up around 25% of chefs and around 75% of waiting staff.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.bha.org.uk/hospitality-tourism-industry-announces-first-post-brexit-sector-skills-strategy-2/ |title=BHA report |access-date=2024-01-26 |archive-date=2017-09-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170911073320/http://www.bha.org.uk/hospitality-tourism-industry-announces-first-post-brexit-sector-skills-strategy-2/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Employer Immigration Services {{!}} Employ Overseas Workers |url=https://www.wmimmigration.com/employer-services/ |access-date=2022-01-19 |website=www.wmimmigration.com |language=en-GB}}</ref> In 2019, 1 in 50 applicants to [[Pret a Manger]] was British.

=== Vietnam ===
The hotel industry in [[Vietnam]] is an important economic sector, contributing significantly to the country's GDP.<ref>{{Cite web |last=dulich.vn |title=Ứng dụng công nghệ trong marketing truyền thông tích hợp cho các khách sạn ở VN |url=https://tcdulichtphcm.vn/suy-ngam/ung-dung-cong-nghe-trong-marketing-truyen-thong-tich-hop-cho-cac-khach-san-o-vn-c8a34059.html |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=Tạp chí Du lịch |language=vi}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=hanoimoi.vn |date=2016-01-27 |title=Du lịch Việt Nam: Lớn mạnh nhờ thay đổi tư duy |url=https://hanoimoi.vn/du-lich-viet-nam-lon-manh-nho-thay-doi-tu-duy-420597.html |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=hanoimoi.vn |language=vi}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-01-27 |title=Du lịch đóng góp 6,6% GDP quốc gia |url=https://mof.gov.vn/webcenter/portal/vclvcstc/pages_r/l/chi-tiet-tin?dDocName=MOF158049 |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=Bộ Tài chính |language=vi}}</ref> According to statistics from the [[Vietnam National Administration of Tourism]], in 2022, Vietnam had a total of 32,313 accommodation establishments<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cả nước có thêm 20 cơ sở lưu trú 4-5 sao với 7.275 buồng |url=https://baodautu.vn/ca-nuoc-co-them-20-co-so-luu-tru-4-5-sao-voi-7275-buong-d193129.html |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=baodautu |language=vi}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Việt/nhadautu.vn |first=Theo Đăng |date=2022-09-08 |title=Ngành Du lịch tăng trưởng mạnh nhờ chuyển đổi số |url=https://tapchitaichinh.vn/nganh-du-lich-tang-truong-manh-nho-chuyen-doi-so.html |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=Tạp chí Tài chính |language=vi}}</ref> with 611,352 rooms, including 1,576 hotels with three stars or higher with 334,487 rooms.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mai - |first=Ban |date=2023-02-14 |title=Khách quốc tế sẽ làm "nóng" ngành khách sạn |url=https://vneconomy.vn/khach-quoc-te-se-lam-nong-nganh-khach-san.htm |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=Nhịp sống kinh tế Việt Nam & Thế giới |language=vi}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=VTV |first=BAO DIEN TU |date=2023-03-24 |title=Khách sạn vừa và nhỏ tại TP Hồ Chí Minh muốn được 'trỗi dậy' nhờ chuyển đổi số |url=https://vtv.vn/news-20230324105450.htm |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=BAO DIEN TU VTV |language=vi}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Mai - |first=Ban |date=2023-08-15 |title=Khách sạn "trông chờ" nguồn khách nội địa |url=https://vneconomy.vn/khach-san-trong-cho-nguon-khach-noi-dia.htm |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=Nhịp sống kinh tế Việt Nam & Thế giới |language=vi}}</ref> Despite this, the Vietnamese hotel industry is still considered to have great potential for development in the future.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trải nghiệm xanh: Lộ trình đến tương lai của ngành khách sạn Việt Nam {{!}} Du lịch |url=https://diendandoanhnghiep.vn/trai-nghiem-xanh-lo-trinh-den-tuong-lai-cua-nganh-khach-san-viet-nam-254157.html |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=diendandoanhnghiep.vn |language=vi}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Bất động sản du lịch, nghỉ dưỡng có nhiều tiềm năng phát triển |url=https://mof.gov.vn/webcenter/portal/ttpltc/pages_r/l/chi-tiet-tin-ttpltc?dDocName=UCMTMP118128 |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=mof.gov.vn}}</ref> According to the forecast of the [[World Tourism Organization]] (UNWTO), Vietnam will be one of the top tourist destinations in the world in the coming years.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tổ chức Du lịch thế giới công bố những dấu ấn của du lịch toàn cầu |url=https://vietnamtourism.gov.vn/post/29606 |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=vietnamtourism.gov.vn}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Tổ chức Du lịch thế giới (UNWTO): Du lịch nội địa và gần nhà là xu hướng nổi bật trong năm 2021 |url=https://vietnamtourism.gov.vn/post/35616 |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=vietnamtourism.gov.vn}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=baochinhphu.vn |date=2023-03-03 |title=Việt Nam là điểm đến ưa thích của du khách quốc tế |url=https://baochinhphu.vn/viet-nam-la-diem-den-uu-thich-cua-du-khach-quoc-te-102230302212630542.htm |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=baochinhphu.vn |language=vi}}</ref> This will create opportunities for the development of the Vietnamese hotel industry.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-12-15 |title=Triển vọng ngành du lịch - khách sạn sẽ khả quan hơn trong năm 2024 |url=https://baodauthau.vn/post-147965.html |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=Báo Đấu thầu |language=vi}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=VnExpress |title=Best Hotel Group In Vietnam |url=https://gmhospitalitygroup.com/ |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=vnexpress.net |language=vi}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Sơn - ======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Indoor mold
======================================================================

{{Use american english|date=October 2022}}
{{Short description|Interior fungal growth}}
[[File:Indoor Mold.jpg|thumb|350px|Indoor mold on the head jamb of the window in a multi-story building]]{{For|the white fungal growth|Mildew}}
'''Indoor mold''' (American English) or '''indoor mould''' (British English), also referred to as [[mildew]], is a fungal growth that develops on wet materials in interior spaces. [[Mold]] is a natural, ubiquitous part of the environment and plays an important part in nature by breaking down dead [[organic matter]] such as fallen leaves and dead trees; indoors, mold growth should be avoided as it can affect the structural integrity of buildings and pose potential health risks to susceptible individuals.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Hardin |first1=B. D. |last2=Kelman |first2=B. J |last3=Saxon |first3=A. |date=May 2003 |title=Adverse human health effects associated with molds in the indoor environment |url=https://doi.org/10.1097/00043764-200305000-00006 |journal=Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine |volume=45 |issue=5 |pages=470–478|doi=10.1097/00043764-200305000-00006 |pmid=12762072 |bibcode=2003JOEM...45..470. |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Mold reproduces by means of tiny [[spore]]s, which range in size from 1 to 40 microns. The spores are like [[seed]]s—but invisible to the naked eye—that float through the air and deposit on surfaces. When the temperature, moisture, and available nutrient conditions are correct, the spores can form into new mold colonies where they are deposited.<ref>{{cite web|date=September 1, 2015|title=Indoor Environmental Quality: Dampness and Mold in Buildings – NIOSH Workplace Safety and Health Topic|url=https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/mold/testing-remediation/|url-status=live|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]]|archive-date=June 25, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250625160334/https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/mold/testing-remediation/}}</ref> There are many types of mold, but all require moisture and a food source for growth. Common indoor molds include ''[[Aspergillus]]'', ''[[Cladosporium]]'', ''[[Penicillium]]'', and ''[[Stachybotrys chartarum]]'', which contribute to respiratory issues and [[allergic reactions]] in sensitive individuals.

==Health effects==
{{Main|Mold health issues}}
Indoor mold is generally not regarded as a dominant allergen that affects healthy individuals.<ref name=":1" /> However, mold exposure can lead to a range of [[Health effect|health effects]], with sensitivity differing from person to person. Indeed, the health impact of its exposure depends on factors such as duration, concentration, and type of exposure, which can influence an individual's susceptibility over time. Prolonged exposure and high level of mold exposure can increase the risk of allergic reactions and [[Respiratory disease|respiratory diseases]], such as [[asthma]], [[allergic rhinitis]], and [[hypersensitivity pneumonitis]]. In fact, studies indicate that more than half of adult workers in moldy/humid buildings suffer from nasal or sinus symptoms due to mold exposure.<ref name="pmid211963492">{{cite journal |vauthors=Park J, Cox-Ganser JM |year=2011 |title=Meta-Mold exposure and respiratory health in damp indoor environments |journal=[[Frontiers in Bioscience]] |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=757–771 |doi=10.2741/e284 |pmid=21196349 |doi-access=free}}</ref> 

While the risk of infections caused by indoor mold is generally low for healthy individuals, certain populations are more vulnerable.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hurraß |first1=Julia |last2=Heinzow |first2=Birger |last3=Aurbach |first3=Ute |last4=Bergmann |first4=Karl-Christian |last5=Bufe |first5=Albrecht |last6=Buzina |first6=Walter |last7=Cornely |first7=Oliver A. |last8=Engelhart |first8=Steffen |last9=Fischer |first9=Guido |last10=Gabrio |first10=Thomas |last11=Heinz |first11=Werner |last12=Herr |first12=Caroline E. W. |last13=Kleine-Tebbe |first13=Jörg |last14=Klimek |first14=Ludger |last15=Köberle |first15=Martin |date=2017-04-01 |title=Medical diagnostics for indoor mold exposure |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1438463916305612 |journal=International Journal of Hygiene and Environmental Health |volume=220 |issue=2, Part B |pages=305–328 |doi=10.1016/j.ijheh.2016.11.012 |pmid=27986496 |bibcode=2017IJHEH.220..305H |issn=1438-4639|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Immunodeficiency|Immunocompromised]] people and those with chronic [[lung]] illnesses, such as [[obstructive lung disease]], are at higher risk for mold allergies and may get serious [[infection]]s in their lungs when they are exposed to [[mold]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kosmidis |first1=C. |last2=Hashad |first2=R. |last3=Mathioudakis |first3=A. G. |last4=McCahery |first4=T. |last5=Richardson |first5=M. D. |last6=Vestbo |first6=J. |date=2023-09-01 |title=Impact of self-reported environmental mould exposure on COPD outcomes |journal=Pulmonology |volume=29 |issue=5 |pages=375–384 |doi=10.1016/j.pulmoe.2021.05.003 |pmid=34130917 |issn=2531-0437|doi-access=free }}</ref> To minimize risks, individuals in these groups should avoid environments prone to mold growth, such as [[compost]] piles, cut grass, and wooded areas.<ref>{{cite web |date=September 5, 2017 |title=Mold – General Information – Facts About Mold and Dampness |url=https://www.cdc.gov/mold/dampness_facts.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191216124251/https://www.cdc.gov/mold/dampness_facts.htm |archive-date=December 16, 2019 |access-date=May 17, 2021 |website=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]]}}</ref> 

===<span class="anchor" id="Symptoms of mold exposure"></span>Symptoms===
Common symptoms of mold exposure may include [[nasal congestion]]; [[sinusitis]]; [[rhinorrhea]], [[Irritation#Eye irritation|eye irritation]]; respiratory difficulties, such as [[Wheeze|wheezing]], [[chest pain]], [[cough]], and persistent [[Sneeze|sneezing]]; [[throat irritation]]; [[Irritation#Skin|skin irritation]], such as a [[rash]]; and [[headache]].<ref>{{cite web|last=|title=Mold and Moisture in Homes|url=https://www.health.state.mn.us/divs/eh/indoorair/mold/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190126174508/https://www.health.state.mn.us/divs/eh/indoorair/mold/|archive-date=January 26, 2019|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=[[Minnesota Department of Health]]}}</ref> Damp indoor environments correlate with upper-respiratory-tract symptoms, such as [[coughing]] and [[wheezing]] in people with [[asthma]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |url=https://www.euro.who.int/__data/assets/pdf_file/0017/43325/E92645.pdf |title=WHO Guidelines for Indoor Air Quality: Dampness and Mould |publisher=[[World Health Organization]] |year=2009 |isbn=9789289041898 |location=[[Geneva]] |oclc=609855936 |access-date=May 17, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210425102632/https://www.euro.who.int/__data/assets/pdf_file/0017/43325/E92645.pdf |archive-date=April 25, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==== <span class="anchor" id="Health effects linking to asthma"></span>Asthma ====
While population-based studies in healthy adults provide limited evidence of a direct causal link between mold exposure and asthma development, research strongly supports the connection between mold exposure in a workplace setting and both the incidence and exacerbation of [[occupational asthma]] in adults.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Caillaud |first1=Denis |last2=Leynaert |first2=Benedicte |last3=Keirsbulck |first3=Marion |last4=Nadif |first4=Rachel |date=2018-05-15 |title=Indoor mould exposure, asthma and rhinitis: findings from systematic reviews and recent longitudinal studies |url=https://publications.ersnet.org/content/errev/27/148/170137 |journal=European Respiratory Review |language=en |volume=27 |issue=148 |doi=10.1183/16000617.0137-2017 |issn=0905-9180 |pmc=9489198 |pmid=29769295}}</ref> Similarly, studies in children have shown that infants in homes with mold have a much greater risk of developing [[asthma]] and [[allergic rhinitis]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Clark |first1=Sierra N. |last2=Lam |first2=Holly C. Y. |last3=Goode |first3=Emma-Jane |last4=Marczylo |first4=Emma L. |last5=Exley |first5=Karen S. |last6=Dimitroulopoulou |first6=Sani |date=2023-08-02 |title=The Burden of Respiratory Disease from Formaldehyde, Damp and Mould in English Housing |journal=Environments |language=en |volume=10 |issue=8 |pages=136 |doi=10.3390/environments10080136 |issn=2076-3298 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2023Envi...10..136C }}</ref><ref name="pmid21196349">{{cite journal |vauthors=Park J, Cox-Ganser JM |year=2011 |title=Meta-Mold exposure and respiratory health in damp indoor environments |journal=[[Frontiers in Bioscience]] |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=757–771 |doi=10.2741/e284 |pmid=21196349 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Infants may develop respiratory symptoms as a result of exposure to ''[[Penicillium]]'', a fungal [[genus]]. Infants and individuals with asthma who reside in damp indoor environments may experience persistent coughing or wheezing, which could indicate mold-related respiratory issues.<ref name=":2" />

==<span class="anchor" id="Causes & growing conditions"></span>Causes and growing conditions==
Mold is ubiquitous on Earth and can grow on almost any substance when moisture is present. It reproduces by releasing [[spores]], which are carried by [[air current]]s. When these spores land on a moist surface suitable for life, they begin to grow.<ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first=OAR |date=2014-08-14 |title=Biological Contaminants and Indoor Air Quality |url=https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/biological-contaminants-and-indoor-air-quality |access-date=2026-09-18 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first=OAR |date=2014-07-29 |title=Mold Course Chapter 1: |url=https://www.epa.gov/mold/mold-course-chapter-1 |access-date=2026-07-28 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en}}</ref>

For indoor mold to thrive, three essential factors are required: [[Nutrient|nutrients]]—such as cellulose, commonly found in building materials; [[moisture]]—which initiates the decaying process; and time—mold growth typically begins from 24 to 48 hours after the provision of growing conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mold Web Course - Chapter 1 |url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2014-08/documents/moldcourse.pdf |website=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency}}</ref>

[[File:Black Indoor Mold.jpg|250px|thumb|Black indoor mold growing in a humid bathroom]]

Common [[cellulose]]-based building materials, such as [[plywood]], [[drywall]], [[furring]] strips, finish [[carpentry]], [[cabinetry]], wood framing, composite [[wood flooring]], [[carpets]], and carpet padding provide food for mold. In carpet, organic load such as invisible dust and cellulose are food sources.

Because common [[building material]]s are capable of sustaining mold growth and mold spores are ubiquitous, mold growth in an indoor environment is typically related to water or moisture exposure and may be caused by incomplete drying of flooring materials (such as [[concrete]]). [[Flood]]ing, leaky roofs, poor building maintenance, or indoor [[plumbing]] problems can lead to interior mold growth.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Perryman|first=Oliver|date=May 5, 2021|title=Best Air Purifier for Mold (2021 Reviews Updated)|url=https://dehumidifiercritic.com/best-air-purifier-for-mold/|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=Dehumidifier Critic|archive-date=May 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210517175734/https://dehumidifiercritic.com/best-air-purifier-for-mold/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Indeed, after water damage to a building, mold grows in walls and then becomes [[Dormancy|dormant]] until subsequent high humidity; suitable conditions reactivate mold. [[Water vapor]] often [[Condensation|condenses]] on surfaces cooler than the moisture-laden air, enabling mold to flourish.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Udawattha |first1=Chameera |last2=Galkanda |first2=Himahansi |last3=Ariyarathne |first3=Isuri Shanika |last4=Jayasinghe |first4=G. Y. |last5=Halwatura |first5=Rangika |date=2018-06-01 |title=Mold growth and moss growth on tropical walls |journal=Building and Environment |volume=137 |pages=268–279 |doi=10.1016/j.buildenv.2018.04.018 |bibcode=2018BuEnv.137..268U |issn=0360-1323|doi-access=free }}</ref> This moisture vapor passes through walls and ceilings, typically condensing during the winter in climates with a long heating season. Floors over [[crawl space]]s and basements, without [[vapor barrier]]s or with dirt floors, are mold-prone. The "doormat test" detects moisture from concrete slabs without a sub-slab vapor barrier.<ref>Udawatthe, C. (2016). ''The embodied energy and life cycle costing: A case study on basic dwellings in Sri Lanka''. Retrieved from <nowiki>https://www.academia.edu/38822030/The_embodied_energy_and_life_cycle_costing_A_case_study_on_basic_dwellings_in_Sri_Lanka</nowiki></ref> Inorganic materials, such as metal or [[polished concrete]], do not support mold growth, although surface mold growth is still possible.

Additionally, insufficient ventilation may accelerate moisture buildup. Visible mold colonies may form where ventilation is poorest and on perimeter walls (because they are nearest the [[dew point]]). Mold grows best in warm temperatures, 25 to 30 °C (77 to 86 °F), although growth may occur between 0 and 35 °C (32 and 95 °F).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kuhn |first1=D. M. |last2=Ghannoum |first2=M.A |date=Jan 2003 |title=Indoor Mold, Toxigenic Fungi, and Stachybotrys chartarum: Infectious Disease Perspective |journal=Clinical Microbiology Reviews |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=144–172|doi=10.1128/CMR.16.1.144-172.2003 |pmid=12525430 |pmc=145304 }}</ref>

Removing one of the three requirements for mold growth reduces (or eliminates) new mold growth: moisture, food for the mold spores (for example, dust or [[dander]]), and warmth since mold generally does not grow in cold environments.[[Image:DublinMold.jpg|thumb|right|alt=Bedroom with mold on wall and ceiling|Although this home experienced minor exterior damage from [[Hurricane Katrina]], small leaks and inadequate airflow permitted mold infestation.]]

=== Hidden mold ===
Mold is detectable by smell and signs of water damage on walls or ceiling and can grow in places invisible to the human eye, posing a significant health hazard when exposed for a prolonged time. It may be found behind [[wallpaper]] or [[paneling]], on the inside of [[dropped ceiling]]s, the back of [[drywall]], or on the underside of carpets or carpet padding. Piping in walls may also be a source of mold, since they may leak (causing moisture and condensation).<ref name="EPA mold guide">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=August 13, 2014|title=A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home|url=https://www.epa.gov/mold/brief-guide-mold-moisture-and-your-home|url-status=live|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|archive-date=January 6, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200106221435/https://www.epa.gov/mold/brief-guide-mold-moisture-and-your-home}}</ref> After a flood or major leak, mycotoxin levels are higher, even after a building has dried out.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mold Prevention Strategies and Possible Health Effects in the Aftermath of Hurricanes and Major Floods |url=https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr5508a1.htm |access-date=2025-03-14 |website=www.cdc.gov}}</ref>

If a house has mold, the moisture may originate in the basement or crawl space, a leaking roof or a leak in plumbing pipes.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Moisture Control Guidance for Building Design, Construction and Maintenance |date=December 2013}}</ref> If there are mold problems in a house only during certain times of the year, the house is probably too [[Hermetic seal|airtight]] or too drafty. Mold problems occur in airtight homes more frequently in the warmer months (when humidity is high inside the house, and moisture is trapped), and occur in drafty homes more frequently in the colder months (when warm air escapes from the living area and condenses). If a house is artificially humidified by the use of a [[humidifier]] during the winter, this can create conditions favorable to mold. 

[[Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning]] (HVAC) systems can also serve as hidden breeding grounds for mold, as they can provide all three requirements for mold growth. The [[air conditioning]] system creates a difference in temperature, encouraging condensation. The high rate of dusty air movement through an HVAC system may furnish ample food for mold. Since the air-conditioning system is not always running, warm conditions are the final component for mold growth.

== <span class="anchor" id="Mold prevention and control"></span>Prevention ==
Mold growth can be inhibited by keeping surfaces at conditions that are further from condensation, with relative humidity levels below 75%. This usually translates to a relative humidity of indoor air below 60%, in agreement with the guidelines for [[thermal comfort]] that recommend a relative humidity between 40–60%. Moisture buildup in buildings may arise from water penetrating areas of the [[building envelope]] or fabric, from plumbing leaks, rainwater or groundwater penetration, or from [[condensation]] due to improper ventilation, insufficient heating or poor thermal quality of the building envelope.<ref>{{Cite book |title=BS 5250:2021 - Management of moisture in buildings. Code of practice |date=October 31, 2021 |publisher=British Standards Institution (BSI) |isbn=978-0-539-18975-9}}</ref> Even something as simple as drying clothes indoors on [[Radiator (heating)|radiators]] can increase the risk of mold growth, if the humidity produced is not able to escape the building via ventilation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Madgwick |first1=Della |last2=Wood |first2=Hannah |date=August 8, 2016 |title=The problem of clothes drying in new homes in the UK |url=https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/SS-10-2015-0048/full/html |url-status=live |journal=Structural Survey |language=en |volume=34 |issue=4/5 |pages=320–330 |doi=10.1108/SS-10-2015-0048 |issn=0263-080X |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210507231216/https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/SS-10-2015-0048/full/html |archive-date=May 7, 2021 |access-date=April 11, 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Residential mold may be prevented and controlled by cleaning and repairing [[rain gutter]]s, to prevent moisture seepage into the home; keeping air-conditioning drip pans clean and drainage lines clear; monitoring indoor humidity; drying areas of moisture or condensation and removing their sources; ensuring that there is adequate ventilation by installing an exhaust fan in your bathroom; treating exposed structural wood or wood framing with a fungicidal encapsulation coating after pre-cleaning (particularly homes with a [[crawl space]], unfinished basement, or a poorly-ventilated attic).<ref name="EPA mold guide" />

For a more proactive or aggressive preventive approach, forward-looking infrared (FLIR) thermal imaging can be used to identify hidden moisture pockets, areas of heat loss, and potential leak risks before visible mold growth occurs. This technique helps detect early signs of moisture intrusion that are otherwise invisible to the naked eye, allowing homeowners and inspectors to address problems before they escalate.<ref>{{cite web |title=FLIR Thermal Imaging for Early Mold Prevention |url=https://www.vegasmoldtests.com/flir-thermal-imaging-for-early-mold-prevention |website=Las Vegas Mold Testing |access-date=13 October 2025}}</ref>

== Assessment ==
An observation of the indoor environment should be conducted before any sampling is performed. The area should be surveyed for odors indicating mold or [[bacteria]]l growth, moisture sources, such as [[Water stagnation|stagnant water]] or leaking pipes, and water-damaged [[building material]]s.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Sullivan |first1=John B. Jr. |last2=Krieger |first2=Gary R. |title=Clinical environmental health and toxic exposures |date=2001 |publisher=Lippincott Williams & Wilkins|isbn=0-683-08027-X|edition=2nd |location=Philadelphia |oclc=41606485}}</ref> This can include moving [[furniture]], lifting (or removing) carpets, checking behind wallpaper or paneling, checking ventilation ductwork and exposing wall cavities. Efforts typically focus on areas where there are signs of liquid moisture or [[water vapor]] ([[humidity]]), or where moisture problems are suspected. In many cases, if materials have failed to dry out several days after the suspected water event, mold growth can be suspected even if it is not immediately visible. Often, quick decisions about the immediate safety and health of the environment can be made by these observations before sampling is even needed.<ref name=":12">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PyUSgdZUGr4C |title=Clinical environmental health and toxic exposures |date=2001 |publisher=[[Lippincott Williams & Wilkins]] |isbn=9780683080278 |editor-last=Sullivan |editor-first=John B. |edition=2nd |location=Philadelphia |pages=41606485 |oclc=41606485 |editor-last2=Krieger |editor-first2=Gary R.}}</ref> The [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] (EPA) does not generally recommend sampling unless an occupant of the space has symptoms. In most cases, if visible mold growth is present, sampling is unnecessary.<ref>{{cite web|last=|first=|date=May 13, 2015|title=Mold Testing or Sampling|url=https://www.epa.gov/mold/mold-testing-or-sampling|url-status=live|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|archive-date=April 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210414062353/https://www.epa.gov/mold/mold-testing-or-sampling}}</ref> Sampling should be performed by a trained professional with specific experience in mold-sampling protocols, sampling methods and the interpretation of findings. It should be done only to make a particular determination, such as airborne spore concentration or identifying a particular [[species]].

=== Sampling ===
Before sampling, a subsequent course of action should be determined.

In the U.S., sampling and analysis should follow the recommendations of the [[Occupational Safety and Health Administration]] (OSHA), [[National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health]] (NIOSH), the EPA and the [[American Industrial Hygiene Association]] (AIHA). Types of samples include air, surface, bulk, dust, and swab.<ref name=":12"/>  Multiple types of sampling are recommended by the AIHA, since each has limitations.<ref name="Niemeier">{{Cite journal|last1=Niemeier|first1=R. Todd|last2=Sivasubramani|first2=Satheesh K.|last3=Reponen|first3=Tiina|last4=Grinshpun|first4=Sergey A.|date=2006|title=Assessment of Fungal Contamination in Moldy Homes: Comparison of Different Methods|journal=[[Journal of Occupational and Environmental Hygiene]]|publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]]|volume=3|issue=5|pages=262–273|doi=10.1080/15459620600637333|pmc=2233946|pmid=16595378|bibcode=2006JOEH....3..262N }}</ref>

==== Air sampling ====
{{further|Bioaerosol}}
Air is the most common form of sampling to assess mold levels. Air sampling is considered to be the most representative method for assessing respiratory exposure to mold.<ref name=":03">{{cite book|last1=Viegas|first1=Carla Sofia Costa|title=Exposure to microbiological agents in indoor and occupational environments|last2=Viegas|first2=Susana|last3=Gomes|first3=Anita|last4=Täubel|first4=Martin|last5=Sabino|first5=Raquel|date=2017|publisher=[[Springer Publishing]]|others=Viegas, Carla Sofia Costa,, Viegas, Susana,, Gomes, Anita,, Täubel, Martin,, Sabino, Raquel|isbn=978-3-319-61688-9|location=[[Cham, Switzerland]]|oclc=1005921897}}</ref> Indoor and outdoor air are sampled, and their mold spore concentrations are compared. Indoor mold concentrations should be less than or equal to outdoor concentrations with similar distributions of species. A predominant difference in species or higher indoor concentrations can indicate poor [[indoor air quality]] and a possible [[Hazard#health hazard|health hazard]].<ref name=":12" /> Air sampling can be used to identify hidden mold and is often used to assess the effectiveness of control measures after remediation. An indoor mold air sampling campaign should be performed over the course of at least several days as the environmental conditions can lead to variations in the day-to-day mold concentration. Stationary samplers assess a specific environment, such as a room or building, whereas personal samplers assess the mold exposure one person receives in all of the environments they enter over the course of sampling. Personal samplers can be attached to workers to assess their respiratory exposures to molds on the job. Personal samplers usually show higher levels of exposure than stationary samples due to the "personal cloud" effect, where the activities of the person re-suspend settled particles.<ref name=":03"/> There are several methods that can be used for indoor mold air sampling.{{Clarify|date=April 2025}}

==== Swab and surface sampling ====
[[File:Aspergillus fumigatus.jpg|thumb|Culture dish with [[Aspergillus fumigatus]] colonies, a species commonly found in indoor air]]
Surface sampling measures the number of mold spores deposited on indoor surfaces.  With swab, a [[cotton swab]] is rubbed across the area being sampled, often a measured area, and subsequently sent to the mold testing laboratory. The swab can rubbed on an [[agar plate]] to grow the mold on a [[growth medium]]. Final results indicate mold levels and species located in the suspect area. Surface sampling can be used to identify the source of mold exposure. Molecular analyses, such as [[Real-time polymerase chain reaction|qPCR]], may also be used for species identification and quantification. Swab and surface sampling can give detailed information about the mold, but cannot measure the actual mold exposure because it is not [[Aerosolization|aerosolized]].<ref name=":03"/>

==== Bulk and dust sampling ====
Bulk removal of material from the contaminated area is used to identify and quantify the mold in the sample. This method is often used to verify contamination and identify the source of contamination. Dust samples can be collected using a vacuum with a collection filter attached. Dust from surfaces such as floors, beds, or furniture is often collected to assess health effects from exposure in [[epidemiology]] studies. Researchers of indoor mold also use a long-term settled [[dust collection system]] where a dust cloth or a [[petri dish]] is left out in the environment for a set period of time, sometimes weeks.<ref name=":03" /> Dust samples can be analyzed using culture-based or culture-independent methods. Quantitative PCR is a [[DNA]]-based molecular method that can identify and quantify fungal species. The Environmental Relative Moldiness Index (ERMI) is a numerical that can be used in epidemiological studies to assess mold burdens of houses in the United States. The ERMI consists of a list of 36 fungal species commonly associated with damp houses that can be measured using qPCR.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Vesper|first1=Stephen|last2=McKinstry|first2=Craig|last3=Haugland|first3=Richard|last4=Wymer|first4=Larry|last5=Bradham|first5=Karen|last6=Ashley|first6=Peter|last7=Cox|first7=David|last8=Dewalt|first8=Gary|last9=Friedman|first9=Warren|date=August 2007|title=Development of an Environmental Relative Moldiness Index for US Homes|journal=Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine|volume=49|issue=8|pages=829–833|doi=10.1097/JOM.0b013e3181255e98|pmid=17693779|s2cid=43568045|issn=1076-2752}}</ref><ref name=":03"/> Like swab and surface sampling, bulk and dust sampling can give detailed information about the mold source, but cannot accurately determine the level of exposure to the source.<ref name=":03" />

== Remediation ==
In a situation where there is visible mold and the [[indoor air quality]] may have been compromised, mold remediation may be needed. The first step in solving an indoor mold problem is to remove the moisture source;<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=October 7, 2015|title=What is mold?|url=https://www.epa.gov/mold/what-mold|url-status=live|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|archive-date=April 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210417181926/https://www.epa.gov/mold/what-mold}}</ref> new mold will begin to grow on moist, porous surfaces within 24 to 48 hours. There are a number of ways to prevent mold growth. Some cleaning companies specialize in [[fabric restoration]], removing mold (and mold spores) from clothing to eliminate odor and prevent further damage to garments.

The effective way to clean mold is to use detergent solutions which physically remove mold.  Many commercially available detergents marketed for mold cleanup include an [[antifungal]] agent.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=September 28, 2015|title=Selected EPA-Registered Disinfectants|url=https://www.epa.gov/pesticide-registration/selected-epa-registered-disinfectants|url-status=live|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|archive-date=May 13, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210513200933/https://www.epa.gov/pesticide-registration/selected-epa-registered-disinfectants}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=August 15, 2016|title=List A: Antimicrobial Products Registered with the EPA as Sterilizers|url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2016-12/documents/list_a_sterilizer.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210226061203/https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2016-12/documents/list_a_sterilizer.pdf|archive-date=February 26, 2021|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]}}</ref>

Mold will start to grow once moisture and organic material come together. This can happen anywhere in a property including bathrooms, walls, garages, bedrooms, kitchens, etc. A smell is a good indicator that there is mold growth that needs immediate attention. If not attended to, the growth can spread through the property contributing to adverse health problems and causing secondary damage to the structure and its contents. Significant mold growth may require professional mold remediation to remove the affected building materials and eradicate the source of excess moisture. In extreme cases of mold growth in buildings, it may be more cost-effective to condemn the building than to reduce mold to safe levels.{{Citation needed|date=November 2020}}

The goals of remediation are to remove (or clean) contaminated materials, preventing fungi (and fungi-contaminated dust) from entering an occupied (or non-contaminated) area while protecting workers performing the [[Dust abatement|abatement]].<ref name="NYCguide">{{cite web|date=November 2008|title=Guidelines on Assessment and Remediation of Fungi in Indoor Environments|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/epi/epi-mold-guidelines.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210513193137/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/epi/epi-mold-guidelines.pdf|archive-date=May 13, 2021|access-date=May 17, 2021|publisher=[[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene]]}}</ref>

===<span class="anchor" id="Evaluating mold exposures"></span><span class="anchor" id="HVAC Cleaning"></span><span class="anchor" id="What to wear when removing mold"></span><span class="anchor" id="Dry brushing or agitation device"></span><span class="anchor" id="Dry ice blasting"></span><span class="anchor" id="Vacuumming"></span><span class="anchor" id="Damp wipe"></span><span class="anchor" id="HEPA vacuum"></span><span class="anchor" id="Disposal of debris and damaged materials"></span>Cleanup and removal methods===
The purpose of cleanup is to eliminate mold and remove contaminated materials. Killing mold with a [[biocide]] is insufficient, since [[chemical substance]]s and [[protein]]s causing reactions in humans remain in dead mold. The following methods are used:
* [[Evaluation]]: Before remediation, the area is assessed to ensure safety, clean up the entire moldy area, and properly approach the mold. The [[EPA]] provides the following instructions:<ref name="EPA mold guide" />
* HVAC cleaning: Should be done by a trained professional.<ref>{{cite web|last=NIOSH|date=September 19, 2018|title=Recommendations for the Cleaning and Remediation of Flood-Contaminated HVAC Systems: A Guide for Building Owners and Managers|url=https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/emres/Cleaning-Flood-HVAC.html|url-status=live|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]]|archive-date=May 7, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210507045710/https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/emres/cleaning-flood-hvac.html}}</ref>
* Protective clothing/[[Personal protective equipment|PPE]]: Includes a half- or full-face [[respirator]]. [[Goggles]] with a half-face respirator prevent mold spores from reaching the [[mucous membrane]]s of the eyes. Disposable [[hazmat suit]]s are available to keep out particles down to one micrometer, and [[personal protective equipment]] keep mold spores from entering skin cuts. Gloves are made of [[Natural rubber|rubber]], [[nitrile]], [[polyurethane]], or [[neoprene]].<ref name="EPA mold guide" /><ref name="NYCguide" />
* Dry brushing or agitation device: Wire brushing or sanding is used when microbial growth can be seen on solid wood surfaces such as framing or underlayment (the subfloor).
* [[Dry-ice blasting]]: Removes mold from wood and cement; however, this process may spray mold and its byproducts into surrounding air.
* Wet vacuum: Wet vacuuming is used on wet materials, and this method is one of those approved by the EPA.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.epa.gov/cwa-methods/whole-effluent-toxicity-methods|title=Whole Effluent Toxicity Methods|website=EPA|date=September 2015 |accessdate=January 29, 2025}}</ref> 

* Damp wipe: Removal of mold from [[Porosity|non-porous]] surfaces by wiping or scrubbing with water and a [[detergent]] and drying quickly.
* [[HEPA]] (high-efficiency particulate air) [[vacuum cleaner]]: Used in remediation areas after materials have been dried and contaminated materials removed; collected debris and dust is stored to prevent debris release.
* [[Debris]] disposal: Sealed in the remediation area, debris is usually discarded with ordinary [[construction waste]].

===Equipment===
Equipment used in mold remediation includes:
* [[Moisture meter]] to measure drying of damaged materials;
* [[Hygrometer|Humidity gauge]], often paired with a [[thermometer]];
* [[Borescope]], a flexible tube with a camera at the end, to illuminate potential mold problems inside walls, ceilings and crawl spaces;
* [[Digital camera]] to document findings during evaluation;
* [[Personal protective equipment]] (PPE): [[respirator]]s, [[glove]]s, impervious suit, and [[eye protection]];
* [[Thermographic camera]], infrared thermal-imaging cameras to identify secondary moisture sources.
* [[HEPA|Hepa Vacuum]], also known as High Efficiency Particulate Filter, is commonly used with mold remediation for safely removing any mold spores from the surface and building materials to deter these pores from becoming airborne.

==<span class="anchor" id="Level I"></span><span class="anchor" id="Level II"></span><span class="anchor" id="Level III"></span><span class="anchor" id="Level IV"></span>Protection levels==
During mold remediation in the U.S., the level of contamination dictates the protection level for remediation workers.<ref>{{cite web|date=July 31, 2014|title=Chapter 6 – Containment and Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)|url=https://www.epa.gov/mold/mold-course-chapter-6|url-status=live|access-date=May 17, 2021|website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|archive-date=April 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210429220939/https://www.epa.gov/mold/mold-course-chapter-6}}</ref> Contamination levels have been enumerated as I, II, III, and IV:<ref>{{Cite web |title=SHIB 03-10-10 A Brief Guide to Mold in the Workplace - English {{!}} Occupational Safety and Health Administration |url=https://www.osha.gov/publications/shib101003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250311190154/https://www.osha.gov/publications/shib101003 |archive-date=2025-03-11 |access-date=2025-03-14 |website=www.osha.gov |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Pulp (paper)
======================================================================

{{Short description|Fibrous material used notably in papermaking}}
{{Other uses|Pulp (disambiguation){{!}}Pulp}}
[[File:Zellstoff 200 fach Polfilter.jpg|thumb|Structural fibres of pulp]]
[[File:Florida Pulp and Paper Company mill, Cantonment, Florida.jpg|thumb|Pulp at a [[paper mill]] near Pensacola, 1947]]
'''Pulp''' is a fibrous [[Lignocellulosic biomass|lignocellulosic]] material prepared by chemically, semi-chemically, or mechanically isolating the [[cellulose fiber|cellulosic fibers]] of [[wood]], [[fiber crop]]s, [[Paper recycling|waste paper]], or [[cotton paper|rag]]s. Mixed with water and other chemicals or plant-based additives, pulp is the major raw material used in [[papermaking]] and the industrial production of other [[Pulp and paper industry|paper products]].<ref name="hunter" /><ref name="bier" />

== History ==
{{main|History of paper}}

Before the widely acknowledged invention of [[papermaking]] by [[Cai Lun]] in China around AD 105, paper-like writing materials such as [[papyrus]] and [[amate]] were produced by ancient civilizations using plant materials which were largely unprocessed. Strips of [[Bark (botany)|bark]] or [[Bast fibre|bast]] material were woven together, beaten into rough sheets, dried, and polished by hand.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Spivey|first=Nigel|date=November 1987|title=J. Swaddling (Ed.), Italian Iron Age Artefacts in the British Museum: Papers of the Sixth British Museum Classical Colloquium. London: British Museum, 1986. Pp x + 483, numerous illus. (incl. pls, text figs). {{text|ISBN}} 0-7141-1274-7.|journal=Journal of Roman Studies|volume=77|pages=267–268|doi=10.2307/300639|jstor=300639|s2cid=162420219 |issn=0075-4358}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|date=1998-12-31|title=El diálogo en el español de América|pages=71–92|publisher=Iberoamericana Vervuert|doi=10.31819/9783865278364-004|isbn=978-3-86527-836-4|chapter=El Dialogo en la Historia Hispanoamericana}}</ref> Pulp used in modern and traditional [[papermaking]] is distinguished by the {{Linktext|maceration}} process which produces a finer, more regular slurry of cellulose fibers which are pulled out of solution by a screen and dried to form sheets or rolls.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/technology/papermaking|title=papermaking {{!}} Process, History, & Facts|website=Encyclopædia Britannica|language=en|access-date=2020-04-15}}</ref> The earliest paper produced in China consisted of bast fibers from the [[Paper mulberry|paper mulberry (kozo)]] plant along with [[hemp]] rag and net scraps.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Citation |last=Tsien |first=Tsuen-Hsuin |author-link=Tsien Tsuen-hsuin|series=Science and Civilisation in China: Chemistry and Chemical Technology |volume=5 Part 1|title=Paper and Printing|publisher=Cambridge University Press|page=4|year=1985}}</ref><ref name="Tsien56-58"/> By the 6th century, the mulberry tree was domesticated by farmers in China specifically for the purpose of producing pulp to be used in the papermaking process. In addition to mulberry, pulp was also made from [[bamboo]], [[hibiscus]] bark, [[Pteroceltis|blue sandalwood]], [[straw]], and [[cotton]].<ref name="Tsien56-58">{{Citation |last=Tsien |first=Tsuen-Hsuin |author-link=Tsien Tsuen-hsuin|series=Science and Civilisation in China: Chemistry and Chemical Technology |volume=5 Part 1|title=Paper and Printing|publisher=Cambridge University Press|pages=56–61|year=1985}}</ref> Papermaking using pulp made from hemp and [[linen]] fibers from tattered clothing, fishing nets and fabric bags spread to Europe in the 13th century, with an ever-increasing use of rags being central to the manufacture and affordability of [[rag paper]], a factor in the development of [[printing]].<ref name="hunter">{{Cite book
 | last1 = Hunter
 | first1 = Dard
 | title =Papermaking, the history and technique of an ancient craft
 | year = 1943
 |publisher= Dover
}}</ref> By the 1800s, production demands on the newly industrialized papermaking and printing industries led to a shift in raw materials, most notably the use of [[pulpwood]] and other tree products which today make up more than 95% of global pulp production.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.dovetailinc.org/upload/tmp/1580141175.pdf|title=Tree-free Paper: A Path to Saving Trees and Forests?|last=Bowyer|first=Jim|date=August 19, 2014|access-date=April 15, 2020}}</ref>
{{gallery |title=Five seminal steps in ancient [[China|Chinese]] papermaking outlined in a [[woodcut]]
|File:Making_Paper_1.PNG|Step 1, Harvesting
|File:Making_Paper_2.PNG|Step 2, Cooking
|File:Making_Paper_3.PNG|Step 3, Making sheets
|File:Making_Paper_4.PNG|Step 4, Packaging
|File:Making_Paper_5.PNG|Step 5, Drying
}}

The use of wood pulp and the invention of automatic [[paper machine]]s in the late 18th- and early 19th-century contributed to paper's status as an inexpensive commodity in modern times.<ref name="hunter"/><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Citation|last1=Ragnar|first1=Martin|title=Pulp|date=2014-05-30|encyclopedia=Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry|pages=1–92|publisher=Wiley-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA|doi=10.1002/14356007.a18_545.pub4|isbn=978-3-527-30673-2|last2=Henriksson|first2=Gunnar|last3=Lindström|first3=Mikael E.|last4=Wimby|first4=Martin|last5=Blechschmidt|first5=Jürgen|last6=Heinemann|first6=Sabine}}</ref> While some of the earliest examples of paper made from wood pulp include works published by [[Jacob Christian Schäffer]] in 1765 and [[Matthias Koops]] in 1800,<ref name="hunter" /><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://recipes.hypotheses.org/8447|title=An Early Modern DIY Guide to Making Paper|last=Leong|first=Elaine|website=The Recipes Project|date=2016 |doi=10.58079/tcxz |language=en-US|access-date=2020-04-15}}</ref> large-scale wood paper production began in the 1840s with unique, simultaneous developments in mechanical pulping made by [[Friedrich Gottlob Keller]] in Germany<ref name="eero" /> and by [[Charles Fenerty]] in [[Nova Scotia]].<ref name=":2">[http://www.charlesfenerty.ca/book.html Burger, Peter]''Charles Fenerty and his Paper Invention''. Toronto: Peter Burger, 2007. {{ISBN|978-0-9783318-1-8}} pp.25–30</ref> Chemical processes quickly followed, first with [[J. Roth]]'s use of [[sulfurous acid]] to treat wood, then by [[Benjamin Tilghman]]'s [[United States patent law|U.S. patent]] on the use of [[calcium bisulfite]], Ca(HSO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, to pulp wood in 1867.<ref name="bier"/> Almost a decade later, the first commercial [[Sulfite process|sulfite pulp mill]] was built, in Sweden. It used [[magnesium]] as the [[counter ion]] and was based on work by [[Carl Daniel Ekman]]. By 1900, sulfite pulping had become the dominant means of producing wood pulp, surpassing mechanical pulping methods. The competing chemical pulping process, the sulfate, or [[kraft process|kraft]], process, was developed by [[Carl F. Dahl]] in 1879; the first kraft mill started, in Sweden, in 1890.<ref name="bier">{{cite book |last=Biermann |first=Christopher J. |title=Handbook of Pulping and Papermaking |year=1993 |publisher=Academic Press |location=San Diego |isbn=0-12-097360-X |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/essentialsofpulp0000bier }}</ref> The invention of the [[recovery boiler]], by [[G.H. Tomlinson]] in the early 1930s,<ref name="eero">{{cite book |author= Sjöström, E. |title= Wood Chemistry: Fundamentals and Applications |publisher= [[Academic Press]]|year= 1993}}</ref> allowed kraft mills to recycle almost all of their pulping chemicals. This, along with the ability of the kraft process to accept a wider variety of types of wood and to produce stronger fibres,<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20061208203749/http://www.indiapapermarket.com/history1.asp History of Paper]. indiapapermarket.com</ref> made the kraft process the dominant pulping process, starting in the 1940s.<ref name="bier"/>

Global production of wood pulp in 2006 was 175&nbsp;million tons (160&nbsp;million tonnes).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.metso.com/corporation/home_eng.nsf/FR?ReadForm&ATL=/corporation/articles_eng.nsf/WebWID/WTB-060828-2256F-A001F |title=Pulp production growing in new areas (Global production) |access-date=2007-10-13 |date=September 5, 2006 |publisher=Metso Corporation |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071023105508/http://www.metso.com/corporation/home_eng.nsf/FR?ReadForm&ATL=%2Fcorporation%2Farticles_eng.nsf%2FWebWID%2FWTB-060828-2256F-A001F |archive-date=October 23, 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In the previous year, 63&nbsp;million tons (57&nbsp;million tonnes) of market pulp (not made into paper in the same facility) was sold, with Canada being the largest source at 21 percent of the total, followed by the United States at 16 percent. The [[wood fiber]] sources required for pulping are "45% sawmill residue, 21% logs and chips, and 34% recycled paper" (Canada, 2014).<ref>{{cite book | last = Sixta |first = Herbert |year = 2006 |title = Handbook of Pulp | volume = 1 |chapter= Preface |publisher= Wiley-VCH Verlag & Co KGaA | page = XXIII |isbn= 3-527-30999-3}}</ref> Chemical pulp made up 93% of market pulp.<ref name="market">{{cite web|url=http://www.pppc.org/en/2_0/2_1.html |title=Overview of the Wood Pulp Industry |access-date=2007-10-13 |year=2007 |publisher=Market Pulp Association |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071016110156/http://pppc.org/en/2_0/2_1.html |archive-date=2007-10-16 }}</ref>

==Wood pulp==
[[File:Paperfibersar.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|Fibres in wood pulp]]
The [[timber]] resources used to make wood pulp are referred to as [[pulpwood]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FyQnAQAAMAAJ&q=pulpwood+timber+used+to+make+wood+pulp|title=Michigan Timber Production: Now and in 1985|last1=Manthy|first1=Robert S.|last2=James|first2=Lee Morton|last3=Huber|first3=Henry H.|date=1973|publisher=Michigan State University, Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension service|language=en}}</ref> While in theory any tree can be used for pulp-making, [[coniferous trees]] are preferred because the cellulose fibers in the pulp of these species are longer, and therefore make stronger paper.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.madehow.com/Volume-2/Paper.html|title=Paper|website=How Products are Made}}</ref>
Some of the most commonly used trees for paper making include [[softwood]]s such as [[spruce]], [[pine]], [[fir]], [[larch]] and [[Tsuga|hemlock]], and [[hardwood]]s such as [[eucalyptus]], [[aspen]] and [[birch]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fhUHBgAAQBAJ&q=Wood+pulp+comes+from+softwood+trees&pg=PA159|title=Agricultural Finance: From Crops to Land, Water and Infrastructure|last=Geman|first=Helyette|date=2014-12-29|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9781118827376|language=en}}</ref> There is also increasing interest in [[Genetically modified tree|genetically modified tree species]] (such as GM [[eucalyptus]] and GM [[Populus|poplar]]) because of several major benefits these can provide, such as increased ease of breaking down lignin and increased growth rate.

A [[pulp mill]] is a manufacturing facility that converts wood chips or other plant fibre source into a thick fiberboard which can be shipped to a [[paper mill]] for further processing. Pulp can be manufactured using mechanical, semi-chemical or fully chemical methods (kraft and sulfite processes). The finished product may be either [[Bleaching of wood pulp|bleached]] or non-bleached, depending on the customer requirements.

Wood and other plant materials used to make pulp contain three main components (apart from water): cellulose fibers (desired for papermaking), [[lignin]] (a three-dimensional polymer that binds the cellulose fibres together) and [[hemicellulose]]s (shorter branched [[carbohydrate]] [[polymer]]s). The aim of pulping is to break down the bulk structure of the fibre source, be it chips, stems or other plant parts, into the constituent fibres.

Chemical pulping achieves this by degrading the lignin and hemicellulose into small, water-soluble molecules which can be washed away from the cellulose fibres without [[Depolymerization|depolymerizing]] the cellulose fibres (chemically depolymerizing the cellulose weakens the fibres). The various mechanical pulping methods, such as groundwood (GW) and refiner mechanical pulping (RMP), physically tear the cellulose fibres one from another. Much of the lignin remains adhering to the fibres. Strength is impaired because the fibres may be cut. There are a number of related hybrid pulping methods that use a combination of chemical and thermal treatment to begin an abbreviated chemical pulping process, followed immediately by a mechanical treatment to separate the fibres. These hybrid methods include thermomechanical pulping, also known as TMP, and chemithermomechanical pulping, also known as CTMP. The chemical and thermal treatments reduce the amount of energy subsequently required by the mechanical treatment, and also reduce the amount of strength loss suffered by the fibres.
